32.110.oldText: "Yes, it's a nice purse... yes, yes," he said, suddenly turning pale. "Take a look, young man."

51.5.oldText: On Hélène's name day, a small gathering of 'just family'—as his wife put it—assembled for supper at Prince Vasili's. All these friends and relatives had been given to understand that the young woman's fate would be decided that evening. The guests took their seats at supper. Princess Kuragina, a stout, imposing woman who had once been beautiful, sat at the head of the table. On either side of her were the most important guests—an old general and his wife, and Anna Pavlovna Scherer. At the other end sat the younger and less important guests, along with family members, and there too sat Pierre and Hélène, side by side. Prince Vasili wasn't eating supper; he circled the table in high spirits, sitting down with one guest after another and making casual, pleasant remarks to each—except to Pierre and Hélène, whose presence he seemed not to notice. He kept the whole party lively. The wax candles burned brightly; the silver and crystal gleamed, as did the ladies' gowns and the gold and silver of the men's epaulettes. Servants in scarlet livery moved around the table; the clatter of plates, knives, and glasses blended with the animated buzz of several conversations. At one end, an old chamberlain was assuring an old baroness of his passionate love for her, at which she laughed. At the other end, someone was telling the story of some poor Mary Viktorovna's misfortunes. In the center, Prince Vasili held everyone's attention. With a playful smile, he was telling the ladies about last Wednesday's meeting of the Imperial Council, at which Sergei Kuzmich Vyazminitov, the new military governor general of Petersburg, had received and read the now-famous letter from Emperor Alexander to Sergei Kuzmich. In it, the Emperor said he was receiving declarations of loyalty from all sides, that the one from Petersburg gave him special pleasure, and that he was proud to lead such a nation and would strive to be worthy of it. The letter began: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides reports reach me...' and so on.

98.5.oldText: "I've known you a long time, you see, and love you like a brother," she said. "How do you find Andrew?" she added quickly, not giving him time to respond to her warm words. "I'm very worried about him. His health was better in winter, but last spring his wound reopened and the doctor said he should go away for treatment. And I'm also very much afraid for him spiritually. He doesn't have a temperament like us women, who can cry away our sorrows. He keeps everything locked inside. Today he's cheerful and in good spirits — but that's the effect of your visit; he's not often like this. If you could persuade him to go abroad... He needs activity, and this quiet, routine life is very bad for him. Others don't notice it, but I see it."

158.0.oldText: Count Rostov took the girls to Countess Bezukhova's. There were a good many people there, but nearly all strangers to Natasha. Count Rostov was displeased to see that the company consisted almost entirely of men and women known for the looseness of their behavior. Mademoiselle George was standing in a corner of the drawing room surrounded by young men. There were several Frenchmen present, among them Metivier, who from the time Helene reached Moscow had been a regular in her house. The count decided not to sit down to cards or let his girls out of his sight and to leave as soon as Mademoiselle George's performance was over.

158.1.oldText: Anatole was at the door, obviously on the lookout for the Rostovs. Immediately after greeting the count, he went up to Natasha and followed her. As soon as she saw him she was seized by the same feeling she had had at the opera — a gratified vanity at his admiration and fear at the absence of any moral barrier between them.

158.2.oldText: Helene welcomed Natasha with delight and was loud in her admiration of her beauty and her dress. Soon after their arrival, Mademoiselle George went out to change her costume. In the drawing room people began arranging chairs and taking their seats. Anatole moved a chair for Natasha and was about to sit down beside her, but the count, who never lost sight of her, took the seat himself. Anatole sat down behind her.

158.3.oldText: Mademoiselle George, with her bare, plump, dimpled arms and a red shawl draped over one shoulder, came into the space left for her and struck an unnatural pose. Enthusiastic whispering was audible.

158.4.oldText: Mademoiselle George looked sternly and gloomily at the audience and began reciting some French verses describing her guilty love for her son. In some places she raised her voice, in others she whispered, lifting her head triumphantly; sometimes she paused and uttered hoarse sounds, rolling her eyes.

158.5.oldText: "Adorable! Divine! Delicious!" was heard from every side.

158.6.oldText: Natasha looked at the plump actress, but neither saw nor heard nor understood anything of what was going on before her. She only felt herself once again completely carried away into this strange, senseless world — so far removed from her old life — a world in which it was impossible to tell what was good or bad, reasonable or senseless. Behind her sat Anatole, and conscious of his nearness she felt a frightened sense of anticipation.

158.7.oldText: After the first monologue the whole company rose and surrounded Mademoiselle George, expressing their enthusiasm.

158.8.oldText: "How beautiful she is!" Natasha remarked to her father, who had also gotten up and was moving through the crowd toward the actress.

158.9.oldText: "I don't think so when I look at you!" said Anatole, following Natasha. He said this at a moment when only she could hear him. "You are enchanting... from the moment I saw you I have never ceased..."

158.10.oldText: "Come, come, Natasha!" said the count, turning back for his daughter. "How beautiful she is!" Natasha, without saying anything, stepped up to her father and looked at him with surprised, questioning eyes.

158.11.oldText: After giving several recitations, Mademoiselle George left, and Countess Bezukhova invited her guests into the ballroom.

158.12.oldText: The count wanted to go home, but Helene begged him not to spoil her impromptu ball, and the Rostovs stayed. Anatole asked Natasha for a waltz, and as they danced he pressed her waist and hand and told her she was bewitching and that he loved her. During the ecossaise, which she also danced with him, Anatole said nothing when they happened to be alone, but simply gazed at her. Natasha lifted her frightened eyes to him, but there was such confident tenderness in his affectionate look and smile that she could not, while looking at him, say what she needed to say. She lowered her eyes.

158.13.oldText: "Don't say such things to me. I'm engaged and I love another," she said quickly... She glanced at him.

158.14.oldText: Anatole was not upset or hurt by what she had said.

158.15.oldText: "Don't talk to me about that! What can I do?" said he. "I tell you I'm madly, madly, in love with you! Is it my fault that you are enchanting?... It's our turn to begin."

158.16.oldText: Natasha, excited and bewildered, looked around with wide, frightened eyes and seemed merrier than usual. She understood hardly anything that went on that evening. They danced the ecossaise and the Grossvater. Her father asked her to come home, but she begged to stay. Wherever she went and whomever she was talking to, she felt his eyes upon her. Later she recalled how she had asked her father to let her go to the dressing room to fix her dress, that Helene had followed her and spoken laughingly of her brother's love, and that she met Anatole again in the small sitting room. Helene had disappeared, leaving them alone, and Anatole had taken her hand and said in a tender voice:

158.17.oldText: "I cannot come to visit you, but is it possible that I shall never see you? I love you madly. Can I never...?" and, blocking her path, he brought his face close to hers.

158.18.oldText: His large, glittering, masculine eyes were so close to hers that she saw nothing but them.

158.19.oldText: "Natalie?" he whispered questioningly while she felt her hands being painfully squeezed. "Natalie?"

158.21.oldText: Burning lips were pressed to hers, and at the same instant she felt herself released, and Helene's footsteps and the rustle of her dress were heard in the room. Natasha looked around at her, and then, red and trembling, threw a frightened look of inquiry at Anatole and moved toward the door.

158.23.oldText: She paused. She so needed a word from him that would explain what had happened and to which she could find no answer.

158.24.oldText: "Natalie, just a word, only one!" he kept repeating, clearly not knowing what to say, and he repeated it until Helene came up to them.

158.25.oldText: Helene returned with Natasha to the drawing room. The Rostovs left without staying for supper.

158.26.oldText: After reaching home, Natasha did not sleep all night. She was tormented by the unanswerable question of whether she loved Anatole or Prince Andrew. She loved Prince Andrew — she remembered distinctly how deeply she loved him. But she also loved Anatole — of that there was no doubt. "Otherwise, how could all this have happened?" she thought. "If, after that, I could return his smile when saying goodbye, if I was able to let it come to that, it means I loved him from the first. It means he is kind, noble, and wonderful, and I couldn't help loving him. What am I to do if I love him and the other one too?" she asked herself, unable to find an answer to these terrible questions.

168.0.oldText: From the end of 1811, an intensified buildup and concentration of the forces of Western Europe began, and in 1812 these forces — millions of men, counting those transporting and feeding the army — moved from the west eastward to the Russian frontier, toward which since 1811 Russian forces had been similarly drawn. On June twelfth, 1812, the forces of Western Europe crossed the Russian frontier and war began — that is, an event took place contrary to human reason and to human nature. Millions of men committed against one another such innumerable crimes, frauds, betrayals, thefts, forgeries, counterfeiting, robberies, arson, and murders as in whole centuries are not recorded in the annals of all the law courts of the world, but which those who committed them did not at the time regard as crimes.

168.1.oldText: What produced this extraordinary event? What were its causes? The historians tell us with naive assurance that its causes were the wrongs inflicted on the Duke of Oldenburg, the failure to observe the Continental System, the ambition of Napoleon, the firmness of Alexander, the mistakes of the diplomats, and so on.

168.2.oldText: Consequently, it would only have been necessary for Metternich, Rumyantsev, or Talleyrand, between a reception and a dinner party, to have taken proper pains and written a more skillful note, or for Napoleon to have written to Alexander: "My respected Brother, I consent to restore the duchy to the Duke of Oldenburg" — and there would have been no war.

168.3.oldText: We can understand that the matter appeared that way to contemporaries. It naturally seemed to Napoleon that the war was caused by England's intrigues (as in fact he said on the island of St. Helena). It naturally seemed to members of the English Parliament that the cause of the war was Napoleon's ambition; to the Duke of Oldenburg, that the cause was the violence done to him; to businessmen, that the cause was the Continental System which was ruining Europe; to the generals and old soldiers, that the main reason for the war was the necessity of giving them employment; to the legitimists of that day, that it was the need of restoring good principles; and to the diplomats, that it all resulted from the fact that the alliance between Russia and Austria in 1809 had not been sufficiently well concealed from Napoleon, and from the clumsy wording of Memorandum No. 178. It is natural that these and a countless number of other reasons — the number depending on the endless diversity of viewpoints — presented themselves to the people of that day; but to us, to posterity, who view the event in all its magnitude and perceive its plain and terrible meaning, these causes seem inadequate. To us it is incomprehensible that millions of Christian men killed and tortured each other either because Napoleon was ambitious or Alexander was firm, or because England's policy was astute or the Duke of Oldenburg was wronged. We cannot grasp what connection such circumstances have with the actual fact of slaughter and violence: why, because the Duke was wronged, thousands of men from the other side of Europe killed and ruined the people of Smolensk and Moscow and were killed by them.

168.4.oldText: To us, their descendants, who are not historians and are not swept up in the process of research and can therefore view the event with unclouded common sense, an incalculable number of causes present themselves. The deeper we delve in search of these causes, the more of them we find; and each separate cause or whole series of causes appears to us equally valid in itself and equally false in its insignificance compared to the magnitude of the events, and in its powerlessness — apart from the cooperation of all the other coinciding causes — to produce the event. To us, the wish or objection of this or that French corporal to serve a second term appears as much a cause as Napoleon's refusal to withdraw his troops beyond the Vistula and to restore the duchy of Oldenburg; for had he not wished to serve, and had a second, a third, and a thousandth corporal and private also refused, there would have been so many fewer men in Napoleon's army and the war could not have occurred.

168.5.oldText: Had Napoleon not taken offense at the demand that he should withdraw beyond the Vistula, and not ordered his troops to advance, there would have been no war; but had all his sergeants objected to serving a second term, there could have been no war either. Nor could there have been a war had there been no English intrigues and no Duke of Oldenburg, and had Alexander not felt insulted, and had there not been an autocratic government in Russia, or a Revolution in France and a subsequent dictatorship and Empire, or all the things that produced the French Revolution, and so on. Without each of these causes nothing could have happened. So all these causes — myriads of causes — combined to bring it about. And so there was no single cause for that event, but it had to occur because it had to. Millions of men, abandoning their human feelings and reason, had to march from west to east to slay their fellows, just as some centuries earlier hordes of men had come from the east to the west, slaying their fellows.

168.6.oldText: The actions of Napoleon and Alexander, on whose words the event seemed to depend, were as little voluntary as the actions of any soldier drawn into the campaign by lot or by conscription. This could not be otherwise, for in order that the will of Napoleon and Alexander (on whom the event seemed to depend) should be carried out, the agreement of innumerable circumstances was needed, without any one of which the event could not have taken place. It was necessary that millions of men in whose hands lay the real power — the soldiers who fired, or transported provisions and guns — should consent to carry out the will of these weak individuals, and should have been induced to do so by an infinite number of diverse and complex causes.

168.7.oldText: We are forced to fall back on fatalism as an explanation of irrational events (that is, events whose reasonableness we do not understand). The more we try to explain such events in history rationally, the more unreasonable and incomprehensible they become to us.

168.8.oldText: Each man lives for himself, using his freedom to achieve his personal aims, and feels with his whole being that he can now do or refrain from doing this or that action; but as soon as he has done it, that action performed at a certain moment in time becomes irrevocable and belongs to history, in which it has not a free but a predetermined significance.

168.9.oldText: There are two sides to the life of every man: his individual life, which is the more free the more abstract its interests, and his elemental hive life in which he inevitably obeys laws laid down for him.

168.10.oldText: Man lives consciously for himself, but serves as an unconscious instrument in the attainment of the historic, universal aims of humanity. A deed done is irrevocable, and its result, coinciding in time with the actions of millions of other men, takes on historic significance. The higher a man stands on the social ladder, the more people he is connected with and the more power he has over others, the more obvious is the predestination and inevitability of his every action.

168.13.oldText: History — that is, the unconscious, general, hive life of mankind — uses every moment of the life of kings as a tool for its own purposes.

168.14.oldText: Though Napoleon at that time, in 1812, was more convinced than ever that it depended on him whether to shed (or not to shed) the blood of his peoples — as Alexander expressed it in the last letter he wrote him — he had never been so much in the grip of inevitable laws, which compelled him, while thinking that he was acting on his own free will, to perform for the hive life — that is, for history — whatever had to be performed.

168.15.oldText: (The French phrase means: "To shed (or not to shed) the blood of his peoples.")

168.16.oldText: The people of the west moved eastward to slay their fellow men, and by the law of coincidence thousands of minute causes aligned and combined to produce that movement and war: complaints about the failure to observe the Continental System, the Duke of Oldenburg's wrongs, the movement of troops into Prussia — undertaken (as it seemed to Napoleon) solely to secure an armed peace, the French Emperor's love and habit of war coinciding with his people's inclinations, the allure of the grand preparations, and the expenditure on those preparations and the need to recoup them, the intoxicating honors he received in Dresden, the diplomatic negotiations which contemporaries believed were conducted with a sincere desire for peace but which only wounded the pride of both sides, and millions of other causes that adapted themselves to the event or coincided with it.

168.17.oldText: When an apple has ripened and falls, why does it fall? Because of its attraction to the earth, because its stalk withers, because it is dried by the sun, because it grows heavier, because the wind shakes it, or because the boy standing below wants to eat it?

168.18.oldText: Nothing is the cause. All this is merely the coincidence of conditions in which all vital organic and elemental events occur. And the botanist who finds that the apple falls because the cellular tissue decays and so forth is equally right with the child who stands under the tree and says the apple fell because he wanted to eat it and prayed for it. Equally right or wrong is he who says Napoleon went to Moscow because he wanted to, and perished because Alexander desired his destruction, and he who says that an undermined hill weighing a million tons fell because the last laborer struck it for the last time with his pickaxe. In historic events, the so-called great men are labels giving names to events, and like labels they have only the smallest connection with the event itself.

168.19.oldText: Every act of theirs, which appears to them an act of their own will, is in a historical sense involuntary and is related to the whole course of history and predetermined from eternity.

169.0.oldText: On the twenty-ninth of May Napoleon left Dresden, where he had spent three weeks surrounded by a court that included princes, dukes, kings, and even an emperor. Before leaving, Napoleon showed favor to the emperor, kings, and princes who had earned it, scolded the kings and princes he was displeased with, presented pearls and diamonds of his own — that is, those he had taken from other kings — to the Empress of Austria, and having, as his historian tells us, tenderly embraced the Empress Marie Louise — who regarded him as her husband, though he had left another wife in Paris — left her grieved by the parting which she seemed hardly able to bear. Though the diplomats still firmly believed in the possibility of peace and worked hard to that end, and though Emperor Napoleon himself wrote a letter to Alexander calling him Monsieur mon frere and sincerely assuring him that he did not want war and would always love and honor him — yet he set off to join his army, and at every station gave fresh orders to speed up the movement of his troops from west to east. He traveled in a coach with six horses, surrounded by pages, aides-de-camp, and an escort, along the road to Posen, Thorn, Danzig, and Konigsberg. At each of these towns thousands of people met him with excitement and enthusiasm.

169.1.oldText: The army was moving from west to east, and relays of six horses carried him in the same direction. On June tenth, coming up with the army, he spent the night in quarters prepared for him on the estate of a Polish count in the Vilkavisski forest.

169.3.oldText: Next day, overtaking the army, he went in a carriage to the Niemen, and changing into a Polish uniform, drove to the riverbank to select a place for the crossing.

169.4.oldText: Seeing on the other side some Cossacks and the wide-spreading steppes in the midst of which lay the holy city of Moscow, the capital of a realm such as the Scythia into which Alexander the Great had marched — Napoleon unexpectedly, and contrary alike to strategic and diplomatic considerations, ordered an advance, and the next day his army began to cross the Niemen.

169.5.oldText: Early in the morning of June twelfth, he came out of his tent, which was pitched that day on the steep left bank of the Niemen, and looked through a spyglass at the streams of his troops pouring out of the Vilkavisski forest and flowing over the three bridges thrown across the river. The troops, knowing of the Emperor's presence, were on the lookout for him, and when they caught sight of a figure in an overcoat and a cocked hat standing apart from his suite in front of his tent on the hill, they threw up their caps and shouted: "Vive l'Empereur!" and one after another poured in a ceaseless stream out of the vast forest that had concealed them and, splitting apart, flowed on and on across the three bridges to the other side.

169.6.oldText: "Now we'll get into action. Oh, when he takes it in hand himself, things get hot... by heaven!... There he is!... Vive l'Empereur! So these are the steppes of Asia! It's a miserable country all the same. Goodbye, Beauche — I'll save the best palace in Moscow for you! Goodbye. Good luck!... Did you see the Emperor? Vive l'Empereur!... If they make me Governor of India, Gerard, I'll make you Minister of Kashmir — that's settled. Vive l'Empereur! Hurrah! hurrah! hurrah! The Cossacks — those rascals — see how they run! Vive l'Empereur! There he is, do you see him? I've seen him twice, as I see you now. The little corporal... I saw him give the cross to one of the veterans... Vive l'Empereur!" came the voices of men, old and young, of the most diverse characters and social positions. On the faces of all was one common expression of joy at the start of the long-expected campaign and of adoration and devotion to the man in the gray coat who was standing on the hill.

169.7.oldText: On June thirteenth, a rather small, thoroughbred Arab horse was brought to Napoleon. He mounted it and rode at a gallop to one of the bridges over the Niemen, deafened by constant rapturous cheering which he clearly endured only because it was impossible to forbid the soldiers from expressing their love for him this way, but which disturbed him and distracted him from the military concerns that had occupied him from the moment he joined the army. He rode across one of the swaying pontoon bridges to the other side, turned sharply to the left, and galloped toward Kovno, preceded by mounted chasseurs of the Guard who, breathless with delight, galloped ahead to clear a path for him through the troops. On reaching the broad river Viliya, he stopped near a regiment of Polish Uhlans stationed by the river.

169.8.oldText: "Vivat!" shouted the Poles ecstatically, breaking their ranks and pressing against one another to see him.

169.9.oldText: Napoleon looked up and down the river, dismounted, and sat down on a log lying on the bank. At a silent signal from him, a telescope was handed to him, which he rested on the back of a happy page who had run up, and he gazed at the opposite bank. Then he became absorbed in a map laid out on the logs. Without lifting his head, he said something, and two of his aides-de-camp galloped off to the Polish Uhlans.

169.10.oldText: "What? What did he say?" was heard in the ranks of the Polish Uhlans when one of the aides-de-camp rode up to them.

169.11.oldText: The order was to find a ford and cross the river. The colonel of the Polish Uhlans, a handsome old man, flushed and stammering with excitement, asked the aide-de-camp whether he would be permitted to swim the river with his Uhlans instead of looking for a ford. In obvious fear of refusal, like a boy asking permission to ride a horse, he begged to be allowed to swim across before the Emperor's eyes. The aide-de-camp replied that probably the Emperor would not be displeased by this excess of zeal.

169.12.oldText: As soon as the aide-de-camp said this, the old mustachioed officer, his face glowing with happiness and his eyes sparkling, raised his saber, shouted "Vivat!" and commanding the Uhlans to follow him, spurred his horse and galloped into the river. He gave an angry kick to his horse, which had grown restive, and plunged into the water, heading for the deepest part where the current was swift. Hundreds of Uhlans galloped in after him. It was cold and frightening in the swift current in the middle of the stream, and the Uhlans grabbed at one another as they fell off their horses. Some of the horses drowned and some of the men; the others tried to swim on, some in the saddle and some clinging to their horses' manes. They tried to reach the opposite bank and, though there was a ford a third of a mile away, were proud that they were swimming and drowning in this river under the eyes of the man who sat on the log and wasn't even looking at what they were doing. When the aide-de-camp, having returned and choosing an opportune moment, dared to draw the Emperor's attention to the devotion of the Poles to his person, the little man in the gray overcoat got up and, having summoned Berthier, began pacing up and down the bank with him, giving him instructions and occasionally glancing disapprovingly at the drowning Uhlans who were distracting his attention.

169.13.oldText: For him it was no new conviction that his presence in any part of the world, from Africa to the steppes of Russia alike, was enough to overwhelm people and drive them to insane self-sacrifice. He called for his horse and rode to his quarters.

169.14.oldText: Some forty Uhlans drowned in the river, though boats were sent to help them. The majority struggled back to the bank from which they had started. The colonel and some of his men got across and with difficulty scrambled out on the far bank. And as soon as they had gotten out, in their soaked and streaming clothes, they shouted "Vivat!" and gazed ecstatically at the spot where Napoleon had been but where he no longer was — and at that moment considered themselves happy.

169.15.oldText: That evening, between issuing one order that the counterfeit Russian paper money prepared for use in Russia should be delivered as quickly as possible and another that a Saxon should be shot on whom a letter had been found containing information about French army orders, Napoleon also gave instructions that the Polish colonel who had needlessly plunged into the river should be enrolled in the Legion of Honor, of which Napoleon was himself the head.

169.17.oldText: ("Those whom God wishes to destroy, He first drives mad.")

170.0.oldText: The Emperor of Russia had meanwhile been in Vilna for more than a month, reviewing troops and holding maneuvers. Nothing was ready for the war that everyone expected and to prepare for which the Emperor had come from Petersburg. There was no general plan of action. The uncertainty about the various plans that had been proposed had only increased after the Emperor had spent a month at headquarters. Each of the three armies had its own commander in chief, but there was no supreme commander of all the forces, and the Emperor did not take on that responsibility himself.

170.1.oldText: The longer the Emperor stayed in Vilna, the less did everyone — tired of waiting — prepare for the war. All the efforts of those surrounding the sovereign seemed aimed merely at making him spend his time pleasantly and forget that war was looming.

170.2.oldText: In June, after many balls and celebrations given by the Polish magnates, by the courtiers, and by the Emperor himself, it occurred to one of the Polish aides-de-camp in attendance that a dinner and ball should be given for the Emperor by his aides-de-camp. This idea was eagerly received. The Emperor gave his consent. The aides-de-camp collected money by subscription. The lady thought most likely to please the Emperor was invited to act as hostess. Count Bennigsen, being a landowner in the Vilna province, offered his country house for the occasion, and June thirteenth was fixed for a ball, dinner, boat race, and fireworks at Zakret, Count Bennigsen's country estate.

170.3.oldText: The very day that Napoleon issued the order to cross the Niemen, and his vanguard drove off the Cossacks and crossed the Russian frontier, Alexander spent the evening at the party given by his aides-de-camp at Bennigsen's country house.

170.4.oldText: It was a gay and brilliant celebration. Connoisseurs declared that rarely had so many beautiful women been assembled in one place. Countess Bezukhova was present among other Russian ladies who had followed the sovereign from Petersburg to Vilna, and outshone the refined Polish ladies with her impressive, typically Russian beauty. The Emperor noticed her and honored her with a dance.

170.5.oldText: Boris Drubetskoy, having left his wife in Moscow and being for the time being a bachelor (as he put it), was also there and, though not an aide-de-camp, had contributed a large sum toward the expenses. Boris was now a rich man who had risen to high rank and no longer sought patronage but stood on equal footing with the most prominent men of his own age. He was meeting Helene in Vilna after not having seen her for a long time and did not dwell on the past, but as Helene was enjoying the favors of a very important personage and Boris had only recently married, they met as good old friends.

170.6.oldText: At midnight the dancing was still going on. Helene, not having a suitable partner, offered to dance the mazurka with Boris. They were the third couple. Boris, coolly looking at Helene's dazzling bare shoulders which emerged from a dark, gold-embroidered gauze gown, talked to her of old acquaintances and at the same time — unaware of it himself and unnoticed by others — never for an instant stopped watching the Emperor, who was in the same room. The Emperor was not dancing; he stood in the doorway, stopping now one couple and now another with gracious words that he alone knew how to deliver.

170.7.oldText: As the mazurka began, Boris saw that Adjutant General Balashev, one of those closest to the Emperor, went up to him and — contrary to court etiquette — stood near him while he was talking to a Polish lady. Having finished speaking to her, the Emperor looked inquiringly at Balashev and, evidently understanding that he acted this way only because there were important reasons for doing so, gave a slight nod to the lady and turned to Balashev. Hardly had Balashev begun to speak before a look of amazement appeared on the Emperor's face. He took Balashev by the arm and crossed the room with him, unconsciously clearing a path seven yards wide as people on both sides made way for him. Boris noticed Arakcheev's agitated face when the sovereign left with Balashev. Arakcheev looked at the Emperor from under his brow and, sniffing with his red nose, stepped forward from the crowd as if expecting the Emperor to address him. (Boris understood that Arakcheev envied Balashev and was displeased that evidently important news had reached the Emperor through someone other than himself.)

170.8.oldText: But the Emperor and Balashev passed out into the illuminated garden without noticing Arakcheev, who, holding his sword and glancing angrily around, followed about twenty paces behind them.

170.9.oldText: All the time Boris was going through the figures of the mazurka, he was preoccupied with the question of what news Balashev had brought and how he could find it out before others. In the figure where he had to choose two ladies, he whispered to Helene that he meant to choose Countess Potocka who, he thought, had gone out onto the veranda, and glided across the parquet toward the door opening into the garden, where, seeing Balashev and the Emperor returning to the veranda, he stopped. They were moving toward the door. Boris, fluttering as if he hadn't had time to withdraw, respectfully pressed close to the doorpost with bowed head.

170.10.oldText: The Emperor, with the agitation of a man who has been personally offended, was finishing with these words:

170.11.oldText: "To enter Russia without declaring war! I will not make peace as long as a single armed enemy remains on my soil!" It seemed to Boris that it gave the Emperor pleasure to utter these words. He was satisfied with the way he had expressed his thoughts but displeased that Boris had overheard them.

170.13.oldText: Boris understood that this was meant for him and, closing his eyes, slightly bowed his head. The Emperor re-entered the ballroom and stayed about another half hour.

170.14.oldText: Boris was thus the first to learn that the French army had crossed the Niemen, and thanks to this was able to show certain important personages that much that was hidden from others was usually known to him, and by this means he rose higher in their estimation.

170.15.oldText: The unexpected news of the French having crossed the Niemen was particularly startling after a month of unfulfilled expectations, and at a ball. On first receiving the news, under the influence of outrage and resentment, the Emperor had found a phrase that pleased him, fully expressed his feelings, and has since become famous. On returning home at two o'clock that night he sent for his secretary, Shishkov, and told him to write an order to the troops and a rescript to Field Marshal Prince Saltykov, in which he insisted on the words being included that he would not make peace so long as a single armed Frenchman remained on Russian soil.

170.16.oldText: The next day the following letter was sent to Napoleon:

170.18.oldText: Yesterday I learned that, despite the loyalty with which I have kept my commitments to Your Majesty, your troops have crossed the Russian frontier, and I have this moment received from Petersburg a note in which Count Lauriston states, as a reason for this aggression, that Your Majesty has considered yourself to be in a state of war with me from the time Prince Kurakin asked for his passports. The reasons on which the Duc de Bassano based his refusal to deliver them to him would never have led me to suppose that could serve as a pretext for aggression. In fact, the ambassador, as he himself has declared, was never authorized to make that demand, and as soon as I was informed of it I let him know how much I disapproved of it and ordered him to remain at his post. If Your Majesty does not intend to shed the blood of our peoples for such a misunderstanding, and consents to withdraw your troops from Russian territory, I will regard what has passed as not having occurred and an understanding between us will be possible. In the contrary case, Your Majesty, I shall see myself forced to repel an attack that nothing on my part has provoked. It still depends on Your Majesty to preserve humanity from the calamity of another war.

173.0.oldText: Though Balashev was accustomed to imperial magnificence, he was amazed at the luxury and splendor of Napoleon's court.

173.1.oldText: The Count de Turenne showed him into a large reception room where many generals, gentlemen-in-waiting, and Polish magnates — several of whom Balashev had seen at the court of the Emperor of Russia — were waiting. Duroc said that Napoleon would receive the Russian general before going for his ride.

173.2.oldText: After some minutes, the gentleman-in-waiting on duty came into the great reception room and, bowing politely, asked Balashev to follow him.

173.3.oldText: Balashev went into a small reception room, one door of which led into a study — the very one from which the Russian Emperor had dispatched him on his mission. He stood a minute or two, waiting. He heard hurried footsteps beyond the door, both halves of it were opened rapidly; all was silent, and then from the study came the sound of other steps, firm and resolute — those of Napoleon. He had just finished dressing for his ride and wore a blue uniform, opening in front over a white waistcoat so long that it covered his round stomach, white leather breeches tightly fitting the plump thighs of his short legs, and Hessian boots. His short hair had obviously just been brushed, but one lock hung down in the middle of his broad forehead. His plump white neck stood out sharply above the black collar of his uniform, and he smelled of cologne. His full face, rather young-looking, with its prominent chin, wore a gracious and majestic expression of imperial welcome.

173.4.oldText: He entered briskly, with a bounce at every step and his head slightly thrown back. His whole short, stout figure, with its broad thick shoulders and chest and stomach naturally jutting forward, had that imposing and stately appearance one sees in well-fed men of forty. It was also evident that he was in the best of spirits that day.

173.5.oldText: He nodded in answer to Balashev's low and respectful bow, and coming up to him at once began speaking like a man who values every moment of his time and does not bother preparing what he has to say, confident that he will always say the right thing and say it well.

173.6.oldText: "Good day, General!" said he. "I have received the letter you brought from the Emperor Alexander and am very glad to see you." He glanced with his large eyes into Balashev's face and immediately looked past him.

173.7.oldText: It was plain that Balashev's personality did not interest him at all. Clearly only what took place within his own mind interested him. Nothing outside himself had any significance for him, because everything in the world, it seemed to him, depended entirely on his will.

173.8.oldText: "I do not, and did not, desire war," he continued, "but it has been forced on me. Even now" (he stressed the word) "I am ready to receive any explanations you can give me."

173.9.oldText: And he began clearly and concisely to explain his reasons for dissatisfaction with the Russian government. Judging by the calmly moderate and friendly tone in which the French Emperor spoke, Balashev was firmly convinced that he wished for peace and intended to enter into negotiations.

173.10.oldText: When Napoleon, having finished speaking, looked inquiringly at the Russian envoy, Balashev began a speech he had long prepared: "Sire! The Emperor, my master..." but the sight of the Emperor's eyes fixed on him confused him. "You are flustered — compose yourself!" Napoleon seemed to say, as with a barely perceptible smile he looked at Balashev's uniform and sword.

173.11.oldText: Balashev recovered himself and began to speak. He said that the Emperor Alexander did not consider Kurakin's demand for his passports a sufficient cause for war; that Kurakin had acted on his own initiative and without his sovereign's consent; that the Emperor Alexander did not desire war and had no dealings with England.

173.12.oldText: "Not yet!" interjected Napoleon, and as if afraid of giving vent to his feelings, he frowned and nodded slightly as a sign that Balashev might continue.

173.13.oldText: After saying all he had been instructed to say, Balashev added that the Emperor Alexander wished for peace but would not enter into negotiations except on condition that... Here Balashev hesitated: he remembered the words the Emperor Alexander had not written in his letter but had specially inserted in the instructions to Saltykov and had told Balashev to repeat to Napoleon. Balashev remembered these words — "So long as a single armed foe remains on Russian soil" — but some complex feeling held him back. He could not utter them, though he wished to. He grew confused and said: "On condition that the French army retreats beyond the Niemen."

173.14.oldText: Napoleon noticed Balashev's embarrassment when uttering these last words; his face twitched and the calf of his left leg began to quiver rhythmically. Without moving from where he stood, he began speaking in a louder tone and more hurriedly than before. During the speech that followed, Balashev, who more than once lowered his eyes, involuntarily noticed the quivering of Napoleon's left leg, which increased the more Napoleon raised his voice.

173.15.oldText: "I desire peace no less than the Emperor Alexander," he began. "Have I not for eighteen months been doing everything to obtain it? I have waited eighteen months for explanations. But to begin negotiations, what is demanded of me?" he said, frowning and making an energetic questioning gesture with his small, white, plump hand.

173.17.oldText: "The Niemen?" repeated Napoleon. "So now you want me to retreat beyond the Niemen — only the Niemen?" repeated Napoleon, looking straight at Balashev.

173.19.oldText: Instead of the demand of four months earlier to withdraw from Pomerania, only a withdrawal beyond the Niemen was now demanded. Napoleon turned quickly and began to pace the room.

173.20.oldText: "You say the demand now is that I should withdraw beyond the Niemen before beginning negotiations, but in exactly the same way two months ago the demand was that I should withdraw beyond the Vistula and the Oder, and yet you are willing to negotiate."

173.21.oldText: He walked in silence from one corner of the room to the other and again stopped in front of Balashev. Balashev noticed that his left leg was quivering faster than before and his face seemed frozen in its stern expression. This quivering of his left leg was something Napoleon was aware of. "The vibration of my left calf is a great sign with me," he remarked at a later date.

173.22.oldText: "Such demands as to retreat beyond the Vistula and Oder may be made to a Prince of Baden, but not to me!" Napoleon almost screamed, quite to his own surprise. "If you gave me Petersburg and Moscow I could not accept such conditions. You say I started this war! But who first assembled his army? The Emperor Alexander, not I! And you offer me negotiations when I have spent millions, when you are in alliance with England, and when your position is a bad one. You offer me negotiations! But what is the point of your alliance with England? What has she given you?" he continued hurriedly, clearly no longer trying to show the advantages of peace and discuss its possibility, but only to prove his own rightness and power and Alexander's errors and duplicity.

173.23.oldText: The beginning of his speech had obviously been intended to demonstrate the advantages of his position and show that he was nevertheless willing to negotiate. But he had started talking, and the more he talked, the less he could control his words.

173.24.oldText: The whole point of his remarks now was clearly to glorify himself and insult Alexander — exactly what he had least wanted at the start of the conversation.

173.26.oldText: Balashev bowed his head in the affirmative.

173.28.oldText: But Napoleon did not let him speak. He clearly wanted to do all the talking himself, and continued with the sort of eloquence and uncontrolled irritability to which spoiled people are prone.

173.29.oldText: "Yes, I know you have made peace with the Turks without getting Moldavia and Wallachia; I would have given your sovereign those provinces, just as I gave him Finland. Yes," he went on, "I promised and would have given the Emperor Alexander Moldavia and Wallachia, and now he won't have those splendid provinces. Yet he might have united them with his empire and in a single reign would have extended Russia from the Gulf of Bothnia to the mouths of the Danube. Catherine the Great could not have done more," said Napoleon, growing more and more excited as he paced up and down the room, repeating to Balashev almost the very words he had used to Alexander himself at Tilsit. "All that, he would have owed to my friendship. Oh, what a splendid reign!" he repeated several times, then paused, drew from his pocket a gold snuffbox, lifted it to his nose, and sniffed at it greedily.

173.31.oldText: He looked compassionately at Balashev, and as soon as the latter tried to speak, hastily interrupted him.

173.32.oldText: "What could he wish for or seek that he would not have obtained through my friendship?" demanded Napoleon, shrugging his shoulders in bewilderment. "But no, he has preferred to surround himself with my enemies — and with whom? With Steins, Armfeldts, Bennigsens, and Wintzingerodes! Stein, a traitor expelled from his own country; Armfeldt, a schemer and a rake; Wintzingerode, a fugitive French subject; Bennigsen, somewhat more of a soldier than the others, but still incompetent — a man who was unable to accomplish anything in 1807 and who should awaken terrible memories in the Emperor Alexander's mind... Granted that if they were competent they might be put to use," continued Napoleon — hardly able to keep pace in words with the rush of thoughts that constantly sprang up, proving how right and strong he was (in his mind the two were one and the same) — "but they are not even that! They are fit neither for war nor for peace! Barclay is said to be the most capable of them all, but I can't say so judging by his first moves. And what are they doing, all these courtiers? Pfuel proposes, Armfeldt argues, Bennigsen deliberates, and Barclay, called on to act, doesn't know what to decide, and time passes with nothing done. Bagration alone is a real soldier. He's stupid, but he has experience, a quick eye, and decisiveness... And what role is your young monarch playing in that ridiculous crowd? They compromise him and put the blame for everything on his shoulders. A sovereign should not be with the army unless he is a general!" said Napoleon, clearly aiming these words directly at the Emperor. He knew how much Alexander wanted to be a military commander.

173.33.oldText: "The campaign started only a week ago, and you haven't even been able to defend Vilna. You are cut in two and have been driven out of the Polish provinces. Your army is grumbling."

173.34.oldText: "On the contrary, Your Majesty," said Balashev, barely able to remember what had been said to him and struggling to follow these verbal fireworks, "the troops are burning with eagerness..."

173.35.oldText: "I know everything!" Napoleon interrupted. "I know everything. I know the number of your battalions as exactly as I know my own. You have not two hundred thousand men, and I have three times that number. I give you my word of honor," said Napoleon, forgetting that his word of honor could carry no weight — "I give you my word of honor that I have five hundred and thirty thousand men this side of the Vistula. The Turks will be of no use to you; they are worthless and have shown it by making peace with you. As for the Swedes — it is their fate to be governed by mad kings. Their king was insane and they replaced him with another — Bernadotte, who promptly went mad — for no Swede would ally himself with Russia unless he were mad."

173.37.oldText: Balashev knew how to reply to each of Napoleon's remarks and would have done so; he continually made the gesture of a man wishing to say something, but Napoleon always interrupted him. To the alleged insanity of the Swedes, Balashev wanted to reply that when Russia is on her side Sweden is practically an island — but Napoleon gave an angry exclamation to drown his voice. Napoleon was in that state of irritability where a man has to talk, talk, and talk, merely to convince himself that he is in the right. Balashev began to feel uncomfortable: as an envoy he feared to compromise his dignity and felt the need to reply; but as a man he shrank before the torrent of groundless fury that had clearly seized Napoleon. He knew that none of the words now uttered by Napoleon had any significance, and that Napoleon himself would be ashamed of them when he came to his senses. Balashev stood with downcast eyes, watching Napoleon's stout legs pace back and forth and trying to avoid meeting his eyes.

173.39.oldText: And probably still more agitated by the fact that he had uttered this obvious lie, and that Balashev still stood silently before him in the same attitude of submission to fate, Napoleon abruptly turned around, drew close to Balashev's face, and gesticulating rapidly and energetically with his white hands, almost shouted:

173.40.oldText: "Know that if you stir up Prussia against me, I'll wipe it off the map of Europe!" he declared, his face pale and distorted by anger, and he struck one small hand energetically against the other. "Yes, I will throw you back beyond the Dvina and beyond the Dnieper, and will rebuild against you that barrier which it was criminal and blind of Europe to allow to be destroyed. Yes, that is what will happen to you. That is what you have gained by alienating me!" And he walked silently several times up and down the room, his plump shoulders twitching.

173.41.oldText: He put his snuffbox into his waistcoat pocket, took it out again, raised it several times to his nose, and stopped in front of Balashev. He paused, looked ironically straight into Balashev's eyes, and said in a quiet voice:

173.43.oldText: Balashev, feeling it his duty to reply, said that from the Russian side things did not look so bleak. Napoleon was silent, still looking at him derisively and clearly not listening. Balashev said that in Russia the best results were expected from the war. Napoleon nodded condescendingly, as if to say: "I know it's your duty to say that, but you don't believe it yourself. I have convinced you."

173.44.oldText: When Balashev had finished, Napoleon again took out his snuffbox, sniffed at it, and stamped his foot twice on the floor as a signal. The door opened, a gentleman-in-waiting, bowing respectfully, handed the Emperor his hat and gloves; another brought him a handkerchief. Napoleon, without looking at them, turned to Balashev:

173.45.oldText: "Assure the Emperor Alexander from me," said he, taking his hat, "that I am as devoted to him as before: I know him thoroughly and very highly esteem his noble qualities. I will detain you no longer, General; you shall receive my letter to the Emperor."

173.46.oldText: And Napoleon went quickly to the door. Everyone in the reception room rushed forward and hurried down the staircase.

175.0.oldText: After his meeting with Pierre in Moscow, Prince Andrew went to Petersburg — on business, as he told his family, but really to find Anatole Kuragin, whom he felt it necessary to confront. On reaching Petersburg he inquired for Kuragin, but the latter had already left the city. Pierre had warned his brother-in-law that Prince Andrew was on his trail. Anatole Kuragin promptly got himself an appointment from the Minister of War and went to join the army in Moldavia. While in Petersburg, Prince Andrew met Kutuzov, his former commander, who was always well-disposed toward him, and Kutuzov suggested that he should accompany him to the army in Moldavia, to which the old general had been appointed commander in chief. So Prince Andrew, having received an appointment on the headquarters staff, left for Turkey.

175.1.oldText: Prince Andrew did not think it proper to write and challenge Kuragin. He felt that if he challenged him without some fresh provocation, it might compromise the young Countess Rostova, and so he wanted to meet Kuragin personally to find a new pretext for a duel. But he again failed to meet Kuragin in Turkey, for soon after Prince Andrew arrived, the latter returned to Russia. In a new country, amid new conditions, Prince Andrew found life easier to bear. After his fiancee had broken faith with him — which he felt the more keenly the more he tried to hide its effects — the surroundings in which he had been happy became painful to him, and the freedom and independence he had once prized so highly were even more so. Not only could he no longer think the thoughts that had first come to him as he lay looking at the sky on the field of Austerlitz and had later developed with Pierre, and which had filled his solitude at Bogucharovo and then in Switzerland and Rome — he even dreaded recalling them and the bright and boundless horizons they had revealed. He was now concerned only with the nearest practical matters unrelated to his past interests, and he seized on these the more eagerly the more those past interests were closed to him. It was as if the lofty, infinite canopy of heaven that had once towered above him had suddenly turned into a low, solid vault pressing down on him, in which all was clear but nothing eternal or mysterious.

175.2.oldText: Of the activities available to him, army service was the simplest and most familiar. As a general on duty on Kutuzov's staff, he threw himself into work with zeal and thoroughness and surprised Kutuzov by his willingness and accuracy. Not having found Kuragin in Turkey, Prince Andrew didn't think it necessary to rush back to Russia after him, but all the same he knew that however long it might be before they met — despite his contempt for Kuragin and all the arguments he devised to prove it wasn't worth stooping to a conflict with him — he knew that when they did meet he would not be able to resist challenging him, any more than a starving man can resist snatching at food. And the awareness that the insult was not yet avenged, that his anger was still unspent, weighed on his heart and poisoned the artificial calm he managed to maintain in Turkey through restless, driven, and rather vainglorious activity.

175.3.oldText: In the year 1812, when news of the war with Napoleon reached Bucharest — where Kutuzov had been living for two months, spending his days and nights with a Wallachian woman — Prince Andrew asked Kutuzov to transfer him to the Western Army. Kutuzov, who was already tired of Bolkonsky's activity, which seemed to reproach his own idleness, very readily let him go and gave him a mission to Barclay de Tolly.

175.4.oldText: Before joining the Western Army, which was then in May encamped at Drissa, Prince Andrew visited Bald Hills, which was directly on his route, only two miles off the Smolensk highway. During the last three years there had been so many changes in his life, he had thought, felt, and seen so much (having traveled both in the east and the west) that on reaching Bald Hills it struck him as strange and unexpected to find the way of life there unchanged, still the same in every detail. He entered through the gates with their stone pillars and drove up the avenue leading to the house as if entering an enchanted, sleeping castle. The same old stateliness, the same cleanliness, the same stillness reigned there, and inside the same furniture, the same walls, sounds, and smell, and the same timid faces, only somewhat older. Princess Mary was still the same timid, plain maiden growing older, uselessly and joylessly passing the best years of her life in fear and constant suffering. Mademoiselle Bourienne was the same flirtatious, self-satisfied girl, enjoying every moment of her existence and full of hopeful plans for the future. She had merely become more self-confident, Prince Andrew thought. Dessalles, the tutor he had brought from Switzerland, wore a coat of Russian cut and spoke broken Russian to the servants, but was still the same narrowly intelligent, conscientious, and pedantic teacher. The old prince had changed in appearance only by the loss of a tooth, which left a noticeable gap on one side of his mouth; in character he was the same as ever, only showing still more irritability and skepticism about what was happening in the world. Little Nicholas alone had changed. He had grown, become rosier, had curly dark hair, and when merry and laughing, quite unconsciously lifted the upper lip of his pretty little mouth just as his late mother used to do. He alone did not obey the law of unchangeability in the enchanted, sleeping castle. But though externally all remained as before, the inner relations of all these people had changed since Prince Andrew had last seen them. The household was divided into two hostile camps that had changed their habits only because he was there and only met because of his presence. To one camp belonged the old prince, Mademoiselle Bourienne, and the architect; to the other, Princess Mary, Dessalles, little Nicholas, and all the old nurses and maids.

175.5.oldText: During his stay at Bald Hills the whole family dined together, but they were ill at ease and Prince Andrew felt that he was a guest for whose sake an exception was being made and that his presence made them all uncomfortable. Involuntarily feeling this at dinner on the first day, he was silent, and the old prince, noticing this, also fell gloomily quiet and retired to his rooms directly after dinner. In the evening, when Prince Andrew went to him and tried to engage him by talking about the young Count Kamensky's campaign, the old prince began unexpectedly talking about Princess Mary, blaming her for her superstitions and her dislike of Mademoiselle Bourienne, who, he said, was the only person truly attached to him.

175.6.oldText: The old prince said that if he was ill it was only because of Princess Mary: that she deliberately worried and irritated him, and that by spoiling and silly talk she was ruining little Prince Nicholas. The old prince knew very well that he tormented his daughter and that her life was very hard, but he also knew that he couldn't help tormenting her and that she deserved it. "Why does Prince Andrew, who sees this, say nothing to me about his sister? Does he think me a villain, or an old fool who, for no reason, keeps his own daughter at a distance and attaches this Frenchwoman to himself? He doesn't understand, so I must explain, and he must hear me out," thought the old prince. And he began explaining why he could not put up with his daughter's unreasonable nature.

175.7.oldText: "If you ask me," said Prince Andrew without looking up (he was criticizing his father for the first time in his life), "I did not wish to speak about it, but since you ask I will give you my honest opinion. If there is any misunderstanding and friction between you and Mary, I can't blame her for it at all. I know how she loves and respects you. Since you ask me," continued Prince Andrew, growing irritable — as he had been prone to do of late — "I can only say that if there are any misunderstandings, they are caused by that worthless woman who is not fit to be my sister's companion."

175.8.oldText: The old man at first stared fixedly at his son, and an unnatural smile revealed the fresh gap between his teeth that Prince Andrew could not get used to.

175.10.oldText: "Father, I did not want to pass judgment," said Prince Andrew in a hard and bitter tone, "but you challenged me, and I have said, and always will say, that Mary is not to blame — the one to blame is that Frenchwoman."

175.11.oldText: "Ah, he has passed judgment... passed judgment!" said the old man in a low voice and, as it seemed to Prince Andrew, with some embarrassment, but then he suddenly jumped up and cried: "Get out, get out! Let not a trace of you remain here!..."

175.12.oldText: Prince Andrew wished to leave at once, but Princess Mary persuaded him to stay one more day. That day he didn't see his father, who didn't leave his room and admitted no one but Mademoiselle Bourienne and Tikhon, but asked several times whether his son had gone. The next day, before leaving, Prince Andrew went to his son's rooms. The boy, curly-headed like his mother and glowing with health, sat on his knee, and Prince Andrew began telling him the story of Bluebeard but drifted into a reverie without finishing it. He thought not of this pretty child, his son whom he held on his knee, but of himself. He searched in himself for either remorse at having angered his father or regret at leaving home for the first time on bad terms with him, and was horrified to find neither. What mattered still more was that he searched for and could not find in himself the former tenderness for his son that he had hoped to reawaken by caressing the boy and taking him on his knee.

175.14.oldText: Prince Andrew, without replying, set him down from his knee and left the room.

175.15.oldText: As soon as Prince Andrew had given up his daily routines, and especially on returning to the old conditions of life amid which he had been happy, weariness of life overcame him with its former intensity, and he hurried to escape these memories and find some work as soon as possible.

175.17.oldText: "Thank God that I can," replied Prince Andrew. "I'm very sorry you can't."

175.18.oldText: "Why do you say that?" replied Princess Mary. "Why do you say that, when you are going to this terrible war, and he is so old? Mademoiselle Bourienne says he has been asking about you..."

175.19.oldText: As soon as she began to speak of that, her lips trembled and tears fell. Prince Andrew turned away and began pacing the room.

175.20.oldText: "Ah, my God! My God! When one thinks who and what — what trash — can cause people misery!" he said with a bitterness that alarmed Princess Mary.

175.21.oldText: She understood that when he spoke of "trash" he was referring not only to Mademoiselle Bourienne, the cause of her misery, but also to the man who had ruined his own happiness.

175.22.oldText: "Andrew! One thing I beg, I implore of you!" she said, touching his elbow and looking at him with eyes that shone through tears. "I understand you" (she looked down). "Don't imagine that sorrow is the work of men. Men are His instruments." She looked a little above Prince Andrew's head with the confident, habitual look of one gazing at a familiar portrait. "Sorrow is sent by Him, not by men. Men are His tools, they are not to blame. If you think someone has wronged you, forget it and forgive! We have no right to punish. And then you will know the happiness of forgiving."

175.23.oldText: "If I were a woman I would do so, Mary. That is a woman's virtue. But a man should not and cannot forgive and forget," he replied, and though until that moment he had not been thinking of Kuragin, all his unspent anger suddenly swelled up in his heart.

175.24.oldText: "If Mary is already urging me to forgive, it means I ought long ago to have punished him," he thought. And giving her no further reply, he began thinking of the glad, vindictive moment when he would meet Kuragin, who he knew was now in the army.

175.25.oldText: Princess Mary begged him to stay one day more, saying that she knew how unhappy her father would be if Andrew left without being reconciled to him, but Prince Andrew replied that he would probably be back soon from the army and would certainly write to his father, but that the longer he stayed now the more bitter their differences would become.

175.26.oldText: "Goodbye, Andrew! Remember that misfortunes come from God, and men are never to blame," were the last words he heard from his sister when he took leave of her.

175.27.oldText: "Then it must be so!" thought Prince Andrew as he drove out of the avenue from the house at Bald Hills. "She, poor innocent creature, is left to be victimized by an old man who has outlived his wits. The old man feels he is guilty but cannot change himself. My boy is growing up and rejoices in life, in which like everybody else he will deceive or be deceived. And I am off to the army. Why? I myself don't know. I want to meet that man whom I despise, so as to give him a chance to kill and laugh at me!"

175.28.oldText: These circumstances of life had been the same before, but then they were all connected, while now they had all collapsed into pieces. Only senseless things, lacking coherence, presented themselves one after another to Prince Andrew's mind.

181.0.oldText: It was nearly three o'clock but no one was yet asleep when the quartermaster appeared with orders to move on to the little town of Ostrovna. Still laughing and talking, the officers began hurriedly getting ready and again boiled some muddy water in the samovar. But Rostov went off to his squadron without waiting for tea. Day was breaking, the rain had stopped, and the clouds were dispersing. It felt damp and cold, especially in clothes still wet. As they left the tavern in the twilight of dawn, Rostov and Ilyin both glanced under the wet and glistening leather hood of the doctor's cart, from beneath which his feet were sticking out, and in the middle of which his wife's nightcap was visible and her sleepy breathing audible.

181.1.oldText: "She really is a dear little thing," said Rostov to Ilyin, who was following him.

181.2.oldText: "A charming woman!" said Ilyin, with all the gravity of a boy of sixteen.

181.3.oldText: Half an hour later the squadron was lined up on the road. The command was heard to "mount" and the soldiers crossed themselves and mounted. Rostov, riding in front, gave the order "Forward!" and the hussars, with clanking sabers and quiet talk, their horses' hoofs splashing in the mud, moved out in fours along the broad road lined with birch trees on each side, following the infantry and a battery that had gone ahead.

181.4.oldText: Tattered, blue-purple clouds, reddening in the east, were scudding before the wind. It was growing lighter and lighter. That curly grass which always grows along country roadsides became clearly visible, still wet from the night's rain; the drooping branches of the birches, also wet, swayed in the wind and flung down bright drops of water to one side. The soldiers' faces grew more and more visible. Rostov, always closely followed by Ilyin, rode along the side of the road between two rows of birch trees.

181.5.oldText: When campaigning, Rostov allowed himself the luxury of riding not a regimental but a Cossack horse. As a judge of horses and a sportsman, he had lately acquired a large, fine, spirited Don horse, dun-colored with a light mane and tail, and when he rode it no one could outrun him. To ride this horse was a pleasure, and he thought of the horse, of the morning, of the doctor's wife, but not once of the approaching danger.

181.6.oldText: Formerly, when going into action, Rostov had felt afraid; now he had not the slightest feeling of fear. He was fearless not because he had gotten used to being under fire (one cannot get used to danger), but because he had learned how to manage his thoughts when in danger. He had trained himself, when going into action, to think about anything except what would seem most likely to interest him — the approaching danger. During the first period of his service, hard as he tried and much as he reproached himself for cowardice, he had been unable to do this, but with time it came naturally. Now he rode beside Ilyin under the birch trees, occasionally plucking leaves from a branch that met his hand, sometimes touching his horse's flank with his foot, or without turning around handing a finished pipe to a hussar riding behind him, all with as calm and carefree an air as though he were merely out for a ride. He glanced with pity at the anxious face of Ilyin, who talked much and in great agitation. He knew from experience the torment of terror and anticipation of death the young officer was going through, and knew that only time could help him.

181.7.oldText: As soon as the sun appeared in a clear strip of sky beneath the clouds, the wind died down, as if it dared not spoil the beauty of the summer morning after the storm; drops still fell, but straight down now, and all was still. The full sun appeared on the horizon and disappeared behind a long narrow cloud above it. A few minutes later it reappeared, brighter still, from behind the top of the cloud, tearing its edge. Everything grew bright and glittered. And with that light, and as if in answer to it, came the sound of guns ahead of them.

181.8.oldText: Before Rostov had time to consider and estimate the distance of that firing, Count Ostermann-Tolstoy's adjutant came galloping from Vitebsk with orders to advance at a trot along the road.

181.9.oldText: The squadron overtook and passed the infantry and the battery — which had also quickened their pace — rode down a hill, and passing through an empty and deserted village ascended again. The horses began to lather and the men to flush.

181.10.oldText: "Halt! Dress your ranks!" the regimental commander was heard ahead. "Forward by the left. Walk, march!" came the command.

181.11.oldText: And the hussars, passing along the line of troops on the left flank of the Russian position, halted behind the Uhlans who were in the front line. To the right stood the Russian infantry in a dense column — the reserve. Higher up the hill, on the very skyline, the Russian guns were visible through the wonderfully clear air, brightly lit by slanting morning sunbeams. In front, beyond a hollow dale, the enemy's columns and guns could be seen. The Russian advance line, already in action, could be heard briskly exchanging fire with the enemy in the dale.

181.12.oldText: At these sounds, long unheard, Rostov's spirits rose, as at the strains of the most stirring music. Tap-tap-tap! the shots cracked, now together, now several quickly one after another. Again all was silent, and then again it sounded as if someone were walking on firecrackers and setting them off.

181.13.oldText: The hussars remained in the same place for about an hour. A cannonade began. Count Ostermann with his suite rode up behind the squadron, stopped, spoke to the regiment's commander, and rode up the hill to the guns.

181.16.oldText: The infantry in front of them split into platoons to let the cavalry pass. The Uhlans started, the streamers on their lances fluttering, and trotted downhill toward the French cavalry visible below to the left.

181.17.oldText: As soon as the Uhlans descended the hill, the hussars were ordered up it to support the battery. As they took the positions vacated by the Uhlans, bullets came from the front, whining and whistling, but fell spent without doing any damage.

181.18.oldText: The sounds, which he had not heard for so long, had an even more pleasurable and exhilarating effect on Rostov than the earlier firing. Drawing himself up, he surveyed the battlefield opening out before him from the hill, and with his whole soul followed the movement of the Uhlans. They swooped down close to the French dragoons; something confused happened there amid the smoke, and five minutes later the Uhlans were galloping back — not to the place they had left but more to the left, and among the orange-colored Uhlans on chestnut horses, and behind them in a large group, blue French dragoons on gray horses could be seen.

183.0.oldText: On receiving news of Natasha's illness, the countess, though not quite well yet and still weak, went to Moscow with Petya and the rest of the household, and the whole family moved from Marya Dmitrievna's house to their own and settled in town.

183.1.oldText: Natasha's illness was so serious that, fortunately for her and for her parents, the question of all that had caused the illness — her conduct and the breaking off of her engagement — faded into the background. She was so ill that it was impossible for them to consider how far she was to blame for what had happened. She couldn't eat or sleep, grew visibly thinner, coughed, and as the doctors made them feel, was in danger. They could think of nothing but how to help her. Doctors came singly and in consultation, talked extensively in French, German, and Latin, blamed one another, and prescribed a great variety of medicines for all the diseases known to them, but the simple idea never occurred to any of them that they could not know the disease Natasha was suffering from, since no disease suffered by a living person can be known — for every living person has his own peculiarities and always has his own unique, personal, novel, complicated disease, unknown to medicine — not a disease of the lungs, liver, skin, heart, nerves, and so on listed in medical textbooks, but a disease consisting of one of the innumerable combinations of ailments of those organs. This simple thought could not occur to the doctors (as it cannot occur to a sorcerer that he is unable to work his spells) because the business of their lives was to cure, and they were paid for it, and had spent the best years of their lives in that business. But above all, this thought was kept from their minds by the fact that they saw they were genuinely useful — as indeed they were to the whole Rostov family. Their usefulness did not depend on making the patient swallow substances that were mostly harmful (the harm was scarcely perceptible, as they were given in small doses), but they were useful, necessary, and indispensable because they satisfied a mental need of the patient and of those who loved her — and that is why there are and always will be pseudo-healers, folk practitioners, homeopaths, and regular doctors. They satisfied that eternal human need for hope of relief, for sympathy, and for the feeling that something should be done — a need felt by those who are suffering. They satisfied the need seen in its most elementary form in a child: when it hurts itself and runs at once to the arms of its mother or nurse to have the sore spot rubbed or kissed, and it feels better when this is done. The child cannot believe that the strongest and wisest of its people have no remedy for its pain, and the hope of relief and the expression of its mother's sympathy while she rubs the bump comforts it. The doctors were of use to Natasha because they kissed and rubbed her bump, assuring her that it would soon pass if only the coachman went to the pharmacy on the Arbat and got a powder and some pills in a pretty box for a ruble and seventy kopecks, and if she took those powders in boiled water at intervals of precisely two hours, neither more nor less.

183.2.oldText: What would Sonya and the count and countess have done, how would they have looked, if nothing had been done — if there had not been those pills to give by the clock, the warm drinks, the chicken cutlets, and all the other details of life prescribed by the doctors, the carrying out of which gave occupation and comfort to the family? How would the count have borne his dearly loved daughter's illness had he not known that it was costing him a thousand rubles, and that he wouldn't grudge thousands more to help her, or had he not known that if her illness continued he wouldn't grudge yet more thousands and would take her abroad for consultations — and had he not been able to explain in detail how Metivier and Feller had not understood the symptoms, but Frise had, and Mudrov had diagnosed them even better? What would the countess have done had she not been able sometimes to scold the patient for not strictly obeying the doctor's orders?

183.3.oldText: "You'll never get well like that," she would say, forgetting her grief in her vexation, "if you won't follow the doctor and take your medicine at the right time! You mustn't trifle with it, you know, or it may turn to pneumonia," she would go on, drawing much comfort from the utterance of that foreign word, incomprehensible to others as well as to herself.

183.4.oldText: What would Sonya have done without the glad consciousness that she had not undressed during the first three nights so as to be ready to carry out all the doctor's instructions precisely, and that she still stayed awake at night so as not to miss the right time to administer the slightly harmful pills from the little gilt box? Even to Natasha herself it was pleasant to see that so many sacrifices were being made for her sake, and to know that she had to take medicine at certain hours, though she declared that no medicine would cure her and that it was all nonsense. And it was even satisfying to be able to show, by disregarding the instructions, that she didn't believe in medical treatment and didn't value her life.

183.5.oldText: The doctor came every day, felt her pulse, looked at her tongue, and regardless of her grief-stricken face, joked with her. But when he had gone into another room, to which the countess hurriedly followed him, he put on a grave expression and thoughtfully shaking his head said that though there was danger, he had hopes of the effect of this latest medicine, and that they must wait and see — that the illness was mainly psychological, but... And the countess, trying to hide the action from herself and from him, slipped a gold coin into his hand and always returned to the patient with a calmer mind.

183.6.oldText: The symptoms of Natasha's illness were that she ate little, slept little, coughed, and was always depressed. The doctors said she couldn't do without medical treatment, so they kept her in the stifling atmosphere of the city, and the Rostovs did not move to the country that summer of 1812.

183.7.oldText: In spite of the many pills she swallowed and the drops and powders from the little bottles and boxes — of which Madame Schoss, who was fond of such things, made a large collection — and in spite of being deprived of the country life she was used to, youth prevailed. Natasha's grief began to be overlaid by the impressions of daily life; it ceased to press so painfully on her heart, gradually faded into the past, and she began to recover physically.

185.0.oldText: At the beginning of July, increasingly alarming reports about the war began to spread through Moscow; people spoke of an appeal by the Emperor to the people and of his coming in person from the army to Moscow. And since by the eleventh of July no manifesto or appeal had been received, exaggerated reports started circulating about them and about Russia's situation. It was said that the Emperor was leaving the army because it was in danger; it was said that Smolensk had surrendered, that Napoleon had an army of a million, and that only a miracle could save Russia.
