185.1.oldText: On the eleventh of July, which was a Saturday, the manifesto was received but had not yet been printed, and Pierre, who was visiting the Rostovs, promised to come to dinner the next day, Sunday, and bring a copy of the manifesto and appeal, which he would get from Count Rostopchin.

185.2.oldText: That Sunday the Rostovs went to Mass at the Razumovskis' private chapel as usual. It was a hot July day. Even at ten o'clock, when the Rostovs got out of their carriage at the chapel, the sultry air, the shouts of street vendors, the light and cheerful summer clothes of the crowd, the dusty leaves of the trees on the boulevard, the sounds of the band and the white trousers of a battalion marching to parade, the rattling of wheels on the cobblestones, and the brilliant, hot sunshine were all full of that summer languor, that mix of contentment and discontent with the present, that is felt most strongly on a bright, hot day in town. All the Moscow elite, all the Rostovs' acquaintances, were at the Razumovskis' chapel, for as if expecting something to happen, many wealthy families who usually left town for their country estates had not gone away that summer. As Natasha, at her mother's side, passed through the crowd behind a liveried footman who cleared the way for them, she heard a young man speaking about her in too loud a whisper.

185.5.oldText: She heard, or thought she heard, the names Kuragin and Bolkonsky. But she was always imagining that. It always seemed to her that everyone who looked at her was thinking only of what had happened to her. With a sinking heart, miserable as she always was now in a crowd, Natasha in her lilac silk dress trimmed with black lace walked—as women can—with all the more poise and dignity the greater the pain and shame in her soul. She knew for certain that she was pretty, but this no longer gave her satisfaction as it used to. On the contrary, it tormented her more than anything lately, especially on this bright, hot summer day in town. "It's Sunday again—another week gone," she thought, remembering that she had been here the Sunday before, "and always the same life that is no life, and the same surroundings in which it used to be so easy to live. I'm pretty, I'm young, and I know that now I am good. I used to be bad, but now I know I am good," she thought, "and yet my best years are slipping by and are no good to anyone." She stood by her mother's side and exchanged nods with acquaintances nearby. Out of habit she sized up the ladies' dresses, criticized the posture of a woman standing close by who wasn't crossing herself properly but in a cramped way, and again she thought with annoyance that she herself was being judged and was judging others, and suddenly, at the sound of the service, she felt horrified at her own sinfulness, horrified that the former purity of her soul was once again lost.

185.6.oldText: A handsome, fresh-looking old man was conducting the service with that gentle solemnity which has such an uplifting and soothing effect on worshipers' souls. The gates of the sanctuary screen were closed, the curtain was slowly drawn, and from behind it a soft, mysterious voice spoke certain words. Tears, the cause of which she herself did not understand, made Natasha's chest heave, and a joyous but overwhelming feeling stirred within her.

185.7.oldText: "Teach me what I should do, how to live my life, how I may become good forever, forever!" she pleaded.

185.8.oldText: The deacon came out onto the raised space before the altar screen and, holding his thumb extended, drew his long hair from under his vestment and, making the sign of the cross on his chest, began in a loud and solemn voice to recite the words of the prayer...

185.10.oldText: "As one community, without distinction of class, without enmity, united by brotherly love—let us pray!" thought Natasha.

185.13.oldText: When they prayed for the warriors, she thought of her brother and Denisov. When they prayed for all traveling by land and sea, she remembered Prince Andrew, prayed for him, and asked God to forgive her all the wrongs she had done him. When they prayed for those who love us, she prayed for the members of her own family—her father and mother and Sonya—realizing for the first time how wrongly she had treated them, and feeling the full strength of her love for them. When they prayed for those who hate us, she tried to think of her enemies and people who hated her, in order to pray for them. She included among her enemies the creditors and all who had business dealings with her father, and always at the thought of enemies and those who hated her she remembered Anatole, who had done her so much harm—and though he did not hate her, she gladly prayed for him as for an enemy. Only in prayer could she think clearly and calmly of Prince Andrew and Anatole, as men for whom her feelings were as nothing compared with her awe and devotion to God. When they prayed for the Imperial family and the Synod, she bowed very low and crossed herself, saying to herself that even if she didn't understand, she could at least not doubt, and in any case she loved the governing Synod and prayed for it.

185.14.oldText: When the deacon had finished the Litany, he crossed the stole over his chest and said, "Let us commit ourselves and our whole lives to Christ the Lord!"

185.15.oldText: "Commit ourselves to God," Natasha inwardly repeated. "Lord God, I surrender myself to Your will!" she thought. "I want nothing, wish for nothing; teach me what to do and how to use my will! Take me, take me!" prayed Natasha, with urgent emotion in her heart, not crossing herself but letting her slender arms hang down as if expecting some invisible power at any moment to seize her and deliver her from herself, from her regrets, desires, remorse, hopes, and sins.

185.16.oldText: The countess looked round several times at her daughter's softened face and shining eyes, and prayed God to help her.

185.17.oldText: Unexpectedly, in the middle of the service, and not in the usual order Natasha knew so well, the deacon brought out a small stool—the one he knelt on during Trinity Sunday prayers—and placed it before the doors of the sanctuary screen. The priest came out wearing his purple velvet cap, adjusted his hair, and knelt down with effort. Everyone followed his example and looked at one another in surprise. Then came the prayer just received from the Synod—a prayer for the deliverance of Russia from foreign invasion.

185.18.oldText: "Lord God of might, God of our salvation!" began the priest in that clear, not showy but gentle voice in which only the Slavic clergy read and which acts so powerfully on the Russian heart.

185.19.oldText: "Lord God of might, God of our salvation! Look this day in mercy and blessing on Your humble people, and graciously hear us, spare us, and have mercy upon us! This foe, laying waste Your land and desiring to devastate the whole world, rises against us; these lawless men are gathered together to overthrow Your kingdom, to destroy Your beloved Jerusalem, Your beloved Russia; to defile Your temples, to overthrow Your altars, and to desecrate our holy places. How long, O Lord, how long shall the wicked triumph? How long shall they wield unlawful power?"

185.20.oldText: "Lord God! Hear us when we pray to You; strengthen with Your might our most gracious sovereign lord, Emperor Alexander Pavlovich; remember his uprightness and meekness, reward him according to his righteousness, and let it preserve us, Your chosen Israel! Bless his counsels, his undertakings, and his work; strengthen his kingdom by Your almighty hand, and give him victory over his enemy, as You gave Moses victory over Amalek, Gideon over Midian, and David over Goliath. Preserve his army, put a bow of brass in the hands of those who have armed themselves in Your Name, and gird them with strength for the fight. Take up the spear and shield and arise to help us; confound and put to shame those who have devised evil against us, may they be before the faces of Your faithful warriors as dust before the wind, and may Your mighty Angel confound them and put them to flight; may they be trapped when they least expect it, and may the plots they have laid in secret be turned against them; let them fall before Your servants' feet and be laid low by our forces! Lord, You are able to save both great and small; You are God, and no man can prevail against You!"

185.21.oldText: "God of our fathers! Remember Your bounteous mercy and loving-kindness which are from of old; turn not Your face from us, but be gracious to our unworthiness, and in Your great goodness and Your many mercies overlook our transgressions and sins! Create in us a clean heart and renew a right spirit within us, strengthen us all in Your faith, fortify our hope, inspire us with true love one for another, arm us with unity of spirit in the righteous defense of the heritage You gave to us and to our fathers, and let not the scepter of the wicked be exalted against the destiny of those You have sanctified."

185.22.oldText: "O Lord our God, in whom we believe and in whom we put our trust, let us not be disappointed in our hope of Your mercy, and give us a sign of Your blessing, that those who hate us and our Orthodox faith may see it and be put to shame and perish, and may all the nations know that You are the Lord and we are Your people. Show Your mercy upon us this day, O Lord, and grant us Your salvation; make the hearts of Your servants rejoice in Your mercy; strike down our enemies and destroy them swiftly beneath the feet of Your faithful servants! For You are the defense, the help, and the victory of those who put their trust in You, and to You be all glory, to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, now and forever, world without end. Amen."

185.23.oldText: In Natasha's receptive state of soul, this prayer affected her powerfully. She listened to every word about the victory of Moses over Amalek, of Gideon over Midian, and of David over Goliath, and about the destruction of "Your Jerusalem," and she prayed to God with the tenderness and emotion that overflowed from her heart, but without fully understanding what she was asking of God in that prayer. She shared with all her heart in the prayer for the spirit of righteousness, for the strengthening of the heart by faith and hope, and its kindling by love. But she could not pray that her enemies be trampled underfoot when only minutes before she had been wishing she had more of them so she could pray for them. Yet neither could she doubt the righteousness of the prayer being read on bended knees. She felt in her heart a devout and trembling awe at the thought of the punishment that falls on people for their sins, and especially her own, and she prayed to God to forgive them all, and her too, and to give them all, and her too, peace and happiness. And it seemed to her that God heard her prayer.

255.0.oldText: Around four o'clock in the afternoon, Murat's troops were entering Moscow. In front rode a detachment of Wurttemberg hussars, and behind them rode the King of Naples himself, accompanied by a large entourage.

255.1.oldText: About the middle of Arbat Street, near the Church of the Miraculous Icon of St. Nicholas, Murat halted to await news from the advance detachment about the condition they had found the citadel—the Kremlin—in.

255.2.oldText: Around Murat gathered a group of those who had remained in Moscow. They all stared in timid bewilderment at the strange, long-haired commander dressed up in feathers and gold.

255.3.oldText: "Is that their Tsar himself? He's not bad!" low voices could be heard saying.

255.5.oldText: "Take off your cap... your caps!" These words went from one to another in the crowd. The interpreter addressed an old porter and asked if it was far to the Kremlin. The porter, listening in perplexity to the unfamiliar Polish accent and not realizing that the interpreter was speaking Russian, did not understand what was being said to him and slipped behind the others.

255.6.oldText: Murat approached the interpreter and told him to ask where the Russian army was. One of the Russians understood the question, and several voices at once began answering the interpreter. A French officer, returning from the advance detachment, rode up to Murat and reported that the gates of the citadel had been barricaded and that there was probably an ambush there.

255.7.oldText: "Good!" said Murat, and turning to one of the gentlemen in his suite, ordered four light guns to be moved forward to fire at the gates.

255.8.oldText: The guns emerged at a trot from the column following Murat and advanced up Arbat Street. When they reached the end of Vozdvizhenka Street, they halted and positioned themselves in the square. Several French officers oversaw the placement of the guns and examined the Kremlin through field glasses.

255.9.oldText: The bells in the Kremlin were ringing for vespers, and this sound troubled the French. They imagined it to be a call to arms. A few infantrymen ran to the Kutafyev Gate. Beams and wooden screens had been put there, and two musket shots rang out from under the gate as soon as an officer and his men began running toward it. A general standing by the guns shouted orders to the officer, who ran back with his men.

255.11.oldText: One shot struck a French soldier's foot, and from behind the screens came the strange sound of a few voices shouting. Instantly, as if at a word of command, the expressions of cheerful confidence on the faces of the French general, officers, and men changed to one of determined readiness for combat and suffering. For all of them, from the marshal to the lowest soldier, that place was no longer Vozdvizhenka, Mokhovaya, or Kutafyev Street, nor the Troitsa Gate—familiar places in Moscow—but a new battlefield that would probably prove bloody. And all made ready for that battle. The cries from the gates ceased. The guns were advanced, the artillerymen blew the ash off their fuses, and an officer gave the word "Fire!" This was followed by two whistling rounds of canister shot, one after another. The shot rattled against the stone of the gate and the wooden beams and screens, and two wavering clouds of smoke rose over the square.

255.12.oldText: A few moments after the echo of the cannon fire resounding over the stone-built Kremlin had died away, the French heard a strange sound above their heads. Thousands of crows rose above the walls and circled in the air, cawing and noisily flapping their wings. Together with that sound came a solitary human cry from the gateway, and through the smoke appeared the figure of a bareheaded man in a peasant's coat. He grasped a musket and took aim at the French. "Fire!" repeated the officer, and the reports of a musket and two cannon shots were heard simultaneously. The gate was again hidden by smoke.

255.13.oldText: Nothing more moved behind the screens, and the French infantry soldiers and officers advanced to the gate. In the gateway lay three wounded and four dead. Two men in peasant coats ran away at the foot of the wall, toward Znamenka Street.

255.14.oldText: "Clear that away!" said the officer, pointing to the beams and the corpses, and the French soldiers, after finishing off the wounded, threw the corpses over the parapet.

255.15.oldText: Who these men were, nobody knew. "Clear that away!" was all that was said of them, and they were thrown over the parapet and removed later so they wouldn't smell. Thiers alone dedicates a few eloquent lines to their memory: "These wretches had occupied the sacred citadel, having armed themselves with guns from the arsenal, and fired" (the wretches) "at the French. Some of them were cut down and the Kremlin was purged of their presence."

255.16.oldText: Murat was informed that the way had been cleared. The French entered the gates and began setting up camp in the Senate Square. Out of the windows of the Senate House, the soldiers threw chairs into the square for fuel and kindled fires there.

255.17.oldText: Other detachments passed through the Kremlin and encamped along Moroseyka, Lubyanka, and Pokrovka Streets. Others settled along Vozdvizhenka, Nikolski, and Tverskoy Streets. Finding no homeowners anywhere, the French were not billeted with inhabitants as is usual in towns, but lived in the city as in a military camp.

255.18.oldText: Though tattered, hungry, worn out, and reduced to a third of their original number, the French entered Moscow in good marching order. It was a weary and famished, but still a fighting and menacing army. But it remained an army only until its soldiers dispersed into their different lodgings. As soon as the men of the various regiments began to spread out among the wealthy, deserted houses, the army was lost forever, and in its place there emerged something that was neither citizens nor soldiers but what are known as marauders. When five weeks later these same men left Moscow, they no longer formed an army. They were a mob of marauders, each carrying a quantity of articles that seemed to him valuable or useful. The aim of each man when he left Moscow was no longer to conquer, but merely to keep what he had acquired. Like a monkey that puts its paw into the narrow neck of a jug, grabs a handful of nuts, and will not open its fist for fear of losing what it holds, and therefore perishes—the French when they left Moscow had inevitably to perish because they carried their loot with them, yet abandoning what they had stolen was as impossible for them as it is for the monkey to let go of its nuts. Ten minutes after each regiment entered a Moscow district, not a soldier or officer was left. Men in military uniforms and Hessian boots could be seen through the windows, laughing and wandering through the rooms. In cellars and storerooms similar men were busy among the provisions, and in the yards they were unlocking or breaking open coach house and stable doors, lighting fires in kitchens, kneading and baking bread with rolled-up sleeves, cooking, or frightening, amusing, or flirting with women and children. There were many such men in both shops and houses—but there was no army.

255.19.oldText: Order after order was issued by the French commanders that day forbidding the men to disperse about the town, strictly forbidding any violence to the inhabitants or looting, and announcing a roll call for that very evening. But despite all these measures, the men who had until then formed an army flowed all over the wealthy, deserted city with its comforts and plentiful supplies. As a hungry herd of cattle keeps together when crossing a barren field but immediately disperses the moment it reaches rich pastures, so did the army disperse all over the wealthy city.

255.20.oldText: No residents were left in Moscow, and the soldiers—like water percolating through sand—spread irresistibly through the city in all directions from the Kremlin into which they had first marched. The cavalry, entering a merchant's house that had been abandoned and finding more than enough stabling for their horses, still went on to the next house which seemed better. Many appropriated several houses, chalked their names on them, and quarreled and even fought with other companies for them. Before they had time to secure quarters, the soldiers ran out into the streets to see the city and, hearing that everything had been abandoned, rushed to places where valuables could be had for the taking. The officers followed to stop the soldiers but were themselves drawn into doing the same. In Carriage Row, carriages had been left in the shops, and generals flocked there to select carriages and coaches for themselves. The few inhabitants who had remained invited commanding officers to their houses, hoping to protect themselves from being plundered. There were masses of wealth and there seemed no end to it. All around the quarters occupied by the French were other areas still unexplored and unoccupied where, they thought, even greater riches might be found. And Moscow engulfed the army ever deeper and deeper. When water is spilled on dry ground, both the ground and the water disappear and mud results; in the same way, the entry of the famished army into the rich and deserted city resulted in fires and looting and the destruction of both the army and the wealthy city.

255.21.oldText: The French attributed the Fire of Moscow to the ferocious patriotism of Rostopchin; the Russians blamed the barbarity of the French. In reality, however, the burning of Moscow could not be attributed to any individual or any group of people. Moscow burned because it found itself in a position where any town built of wood was bound to burn, quite apart from whether it had a hundred and thirty inferior fire engines or not. Deserted Moscow had to burn as inevitably as a heap of shavings must burn when sparks continuously fall on it for several days. A town built of wood, where fires break out almost daily even when homeowners are present and a police force is maintained, cannot help burning when its inhabitants have left and it is occupied by soldiers who smoke pipes, make campfires of Senate chairs in the Senate Square, and cook themselves meals twice a day. In peacetime, merely billeting troops in the villages of any district immediately increases the number of fires. How much more must the probability of fire increase in an abandoned, wooden town occupied by foreign troops? "The ferocious patriotism of Rostopchin" and the barbarity of the French were not to blame. Moscow was set on fire by soldiers' pipes, kitchens, and campfires, and by the carelessness of enemy soldiers occupying houses they did not own. Even if there was any arson (which is very doubtful, since no one had any reason to burn the houses—in any case a troublesome and dangerous thing to do), arson cannot be regarded as the cause, for the same thing would have happened without it.

255.23.oldText: However tempting it might be for the French to blame Rostopchin's ferocity and for the Russians to blame the scoundrel Bonaparte, or later to place a heroic torch in the hands of their own people, it is impossible not to see that there could be no such direct cause of the fire, for Moscow had to burn as every village, factory, or house must burn that is left by its owners and in which strangers are allowed to live and cook their food. Moscow was burned by its inhabitants, it is true, but by those who had abandoned it, not by those who remained in it. Moscow when occupied by the enemy did not remain intact like Berlin, Vienna, and other towns, simply because its inhabitants abandoned it and did not welcome the French with bread and salt, nor bring them the keys of the city.

260.0.oldText: The valet, returning to the cottage, told the count that Moscow was burning. The count put on his dressing gown and went out to look. Sonya and Madame Schoss, who had not yet undressed, went out with him. Only Natasha and the countess remained in the room. Petya was no longer with the family—he had gone on with his regiment, which was heading for Troitsa.

260.1.oldText: The countess, hearing that Moscow was on fire, began to cry. Natasha, pale and with a fixed look, was sitting on the bench under the icons just where she had sat down on arriving, and paid no attention to her father's words. She was listening to the ceaseless moaning of the adjutant, three houses away.

260.2.oldText: "Oh, how terrible," said Sonya, returning from the yard chilled and frightened. "I believe the whole of Moscow will burn, there's an awful glow! Natasha, do look! You can see it from the window," she said to her cousin, evidently wishing to distract her mind.

260.3.oldText: But Natasha looked at her as if not understanding what was said to her and again fixed her eyes on the corner of the stove. She had been in this state of stupor since the morning, when Sonya—to the surprise and annoyance of the countess—had for some inexplicable reason found it necessary to tell Natasha of Prince Andrew's wound and his being with their party. The countess had seldom been so angry with anyone as she was with Sonya. Sonya had cried and begged forgiveness, and now, as if trying to make up for her mistake, paid constant attention to her cousin.

260.4.oldText: "Look, Natasha, how dreadfully it is burning!" said she.

260.6.oldText: And as if simply to get rid of Sonya without offending her, she turned her face to the window, looked out in such a way that it was obvious she could not see anything, and settled back into her former position.

260.8.oldText: "Yes, I really did," Natasha replied in a voice that begged to be left in peace.

260.9.oldText: Both the countess and Sonya understood that, naturally, neither Moscow nor the burning of Moscow nor anything else could seem important to Natasha.

260.10.oldText: The count came back and lay down behind the partition. The countess went up to her daughter and touched her head with the back of her hand as she used to do when Natasha was ill, then touched her forehead with her lips as if to feel whether she was feverish, and finally kissed her.

260.13.oldText: When that morning Natasha had been told that Prince Andrew was seriously wounded and was traveling with their party, she had at first asked many questions: Where was he going? How was he wounded? Was it serious? Could she see him? But after she was told that she could not see him, that he was seriously wounded but that his life was not in danger, she stopped asking questions or speaking at all—evidently not believing what they told her, and convinced that no matter what she said, she would hear the same thing. All the way she had sat motionless in a corner of the coach with wide-open eyes, and the expression the countess knew so well and feared so much was in them. Now she sat in the same way on the bench where she had settled upon arriving. She was planning something and either deciding or had already decided something in her mind. The countess knew this, but what it might be she did not know, and this alarmed and tormented her.

260.14.oldText: "Natasha, undress, darling; lie down on my bed."

260.15.oldText: A bed had been made up on a bedstead for the countess only. Madame Schoss and the two girls were to sleep on some hay on the floor.

260.16.oldText: "No, Mama, I'll lie down here on the floor," Natasha replied irritably, and she went to the window and opened it. Through the open window the moans of the adjutant could be heard more clearly. She put her head out into the damp night air, and the countess saw her slim neck shaking with sobs and throbbing against the window frame. Natasha knew it was not Prince Andrew who was moaning. She knew Prince Andrew was in the same yard as themselves, in a part of the hut across the passage; but this dreadful incessant moaning made her sob. The countess exchanged a look with Sonya.

260.17.oldText: "Lie down, darling; lie down, my pet," said the countess, softly touching Natasha's shoulders. "Come, lie down."

260.18.oldText: "Oh, yes... I'll lie down at once," said Natasha, and began hurriedly undressing, tugging at the tapes of her petticoat.

260.19.oldText: When she had thrown off her dress and put on a dressing jacket, she sat down with her foot tucked under her on the bed made up on the floor, jerked her thin, rather short braid of hair to the front, and began rebraiding it. Her long, thin, practiced fingers rapidly unbraided, rebraided, and tied up her hair. Her head moved from side to side from habit, but her eyes, feverishly wide, stared fixedly ahead. When she was finished getting ready for the night, she sank gently onto the sheet spread over the hay on the side nearest the door.

260.22.oldText: The countess, Madame Schoss, and Sonya undressed hastily and lay down. The small lamp in front of the icons was the only light left in the room. But in the yard there was a glow from the fire at Little Mytishchi, a mile and a half away, and through the night came the noise of people shouting at a tavern Mamonov's Cossacks had set up across the street, and the adjutant's unceasing moans could still be heard.

260.23.oldText: For a long time Natasha listened intently to the sounds coming from inside and outside the room and did not move. First she heard her mother praying and sighing and the creaking of her bed, then Madame Schoss's familiar whistling snore and Sonya's gentle breathing. Then the countess called to Natasha. Natasha did not answer.

260.24.oldText: "I think she's asleep, Mama," said Sonya softly.

260.26.oldText: Soon after that Natasha heard her mother's steady breathing. Natasha did not move, though her small bare foot, sticking out from under the quilt, was growing cold on the bare floor.

260.27.oldText: As if to celebrate a victory over everybody, a cricket chirped in a crack in the wall. A rooster crowed far off and another replied nearby. The shouting in the tavern had died down; only the moaning of the adjutant was heard. Natasha sat up.

260.28.oldText: "Sonya, are you asleep? Mama?" she whispered.

260.29.oldText: No one replied. Natasha rose slowly and carefully, crossed herself, and stepped cautiously on the cold and dirty floor with her slim, supple, bare feet. The floorboards creaked. Stepping cautiously from one foot to the other, she ran like a kitten the few steps to the door and grasped the cold door handle.

260.30.oldText: It seemed to her that something heavy was beating rhythmically against all the walls of the room: it was her own heart, sinking with alarm and terror and overflowing with love.

260.31.oldText: She opened the door and stepped across the threshold onto the cold, damp earthen floor of the passage. The cold she felt refreshed her. With her bare feet she touched a sleeping man, stepped over him, and opened the door into the part of the hut where Prince Andrew lay. It was dark in there. In the farthest corner, on a bench beside a bed on which something was lying, stood a tallow candle with a long, thick, smoldering wick.

260.32.oldText: From the moment she had been told that morning of Prince Andrew's wound and his presence there, Natasha had resolved to see him. She did not know why she had to, she knew the meeting would be painful, but felt all the more certain that it was necessary.

260.33.oldText: All day she had lived only in hope of seeing him that night. But now that the moment had come, she was filled with dread of what she might see. How was he disfigured? What was left of him? Was he like that incessant moaning of the adjutant? Yes, he was that moaning made flesh. When she saw an indistinct shape in the corner and mistook his knees raised under the quilt for his shoulders, she imagined a horrible body there and stood still in terror. But an irresistible impulse drew her forward. She cautiously took one step and then another, and found herself in the middle of a small room filled with baggage. Another man—Timokhin—was lying in a corner on the benches beneath the icons, and two others—the doctor and a valet—lay on the floor.

260.34.oldText: The valet sat up and whispered something. Timokhin, kept awake by the pain in his wounded leg, gazed with wide-open eyes at this strange apparition of a girl in a white nightdress, dressing jacket, and nightcap. The valet's sleepy, frightened exclamation—"What do you want? What's the matter?"—made Natasha approach more swiftly to what was lying in the corner. No matter how unlike a man that body looked, she had to see him. She passed the valet, the snuff fell from the candle wick, and she saw Prince Andrew clearly with his arms outside the quilt, and just as she had always known him.

260.35.oldText: He was the same as ever, but the feverish color of his face, his glittering eyes turned rapturously toward her, and especially his neck—delicate as a child's, revealed by the turned-down collar of his shirt—gave him a peculiarly innocent, childlike look, such as she had never seen on him before. She went up to him and with a swift, flexible, youthful movement dropped to her knees.

261.0.oldText: Seven days had passed since Prince Andrew found himself at the field hospital on the battlefield of Borodino. His feverish state and the inflammation of his injured bowels, the doctor believed, would certainly kill him. But on the seventh day he ate a piece of bread with some tea with pleasure, and the doctor noticed that his temperature was lower. He had regained consciousness that morning. The first night after they left Moscow had been fairly warm and he had remained in the carriage, but at Mytishchi the wounded man himself asked to be taken out and given some tea. The pain caused by being moved into the hut made him groan aloud and lose consciousness again. When he had been placed on his camp bed, he lay for a long time motionless with closed eyes. Then he opened them and whispered softly: "And the tea?" Remembering such a small, everyday detail astonished the doctor. He felt Prince Andrew's pulse and, to his surprise and dissatisfaction, found it had improved. He was dissatisfied because he knew from experience that if his patient did not die now, he would die a little later with greater suffering. Timokhin, the red-nosed major from Prince Andrew's regiment, had joined him in Moscow and was being taken along, having been wounded in the leg at Borodino. They were accompanied by a doctor, Prince Andrew's valet, his coachman, and two orderlies.

261.1.oldText: They gave Prince Andrew some tea. He drank it eagerly, looking with feverish eyes at the door before him as if trying to understand and remember something.

261.3.oldText: Timokhin crept along the bench toward him.

261.6.oldText: "Mine, sir? All right. But how about you?"

261.7.oldText: Prince Andrew pondered again as if trying to remember something.

261.8.oldText: "Couldn't someone get me a book?" he asked.

261.11.oldText: The doctor promised to get it for him and began asking how he was feeling. Prince Andrew answered all his questions reluctantly but reasonably, then said he wanted a bolster placed under him because he was uncomfortable and in great pain. The doctor and valet lifted the cloak covering him and, making wry faces at the terrible smell of mortifying flesh that came from the wound, began examining that dreadful place. The doctor was very much displeased about something and made a change in the dressings, turning the wounded man over so that he groaned again and grew unconscious and delirious from the agony. He kept asking them to get him the book and put it under him.

261.12.oldText: "What trouble would it be to you?" he said. "I don't have one. Please get it for me and put it underneath for a moment," he pleaded in a piteous voice.

261.13.oldText: The doctor went into the passage to wash his hands.

261.14.oldText: "You people have no conscience," said he to the valet who was pouring water over his hands. "I turn my back for one moment... It's such pain, you know, I'm amazed he can bear it."

261.15.oldText: "By the Lord Jesus Christ, I thought we had put something under him!" said the valet.

261.16.oldText: The first time Prince Andrew understood where he was and what had happened, and remembered being wounded, was when he asked to be carried into the hut after his carriage had stopped at Mytishchi. After growing confused from pain while being carried in, he again regained consciousness, and while drinking tea once more recalled everything that had happened to him, and above all vividly remembered the moment at the field hospital when, at the sight of the suffering of a man he disliked, those new thoughts had come to him—thoughts that promised happiness. And those thoughts, though now vague and indefinite, again filled his soul. He remembered that he had a new source of happiness, and that this happiness had something to do with the Gospels. That was why he asked for a copy. The uncomfortable position they had put him in and turned him over again confused his thoughts, and when he came to himself a third time, it was in the complete stillness of the night. Everyone near him was sleeping. A cricket chirped from across the passage; someone was shouting and singing in the street; cockroaches rustled on the table, on the icons, and on the walls, and a big fly buzzed at the head of the bed and around the candle beside him, its wick charred and shaped like a mushroom.

261.17.oldText: His mind was not in a normal state. A healthy person usually thinks of, feels, and remembers countless things simultaneously, but has the power and will to select one sequence of thoughts or events on which to focus all his attention. A healthy person can tear himself away from the deepest reflections to say a polite word to someone who enters, and then return to his own thoughts. But Prince Andrew's mind was not in a normal state in that respect. All the powers of his mind were more active and clearer than ever, but they operated apart from his will. The most diverse thoughts and images occupied him simultaneously. At times his brain suddenly began to work with a vigor, clarity, and depth it had never reached when he was healthy, but suddenly in the midst of its work it would turn to some unexpected idea and he lacked the strength to return to the first.

261.18.oldText: "Yes, a new happiness was revealed to me—one that cannot be taken from a person," he thought as he lay in the semi-darkness of the quiet hut, gazing fixedly before him with feverish, wide-open eyes. "A happiness lying beyond material forces, beyond the material influences that act on a person—a happiness of the soul alone, the happiness of loving. Every person can understand it, but only God could conceive and command it. But how did God command that law? And why was the Son...?"

261.19.oldText: And suddenly the sequence of these thoughts broke off, and Prince Andrew heard (without knowing whether it was a delusion or reality) a soft whispering voice incessantly and rhythmically repeating "piti-piti-piti," and then "titi," and then again "piti-piti-piti," and "ti-ti" once more. At the same time he felt that above his face, above the very middle of it, some strange airy structure was being built out of slender needles or splinters, to the sound of this whispered music. He felt that he had to balance carefully (though it was difficult) so that this airy structure would not collapse; but nevertheless it kept collapsing and again slowly rising to the sound of the whispered rhythmic music—"it stretches, stretches, spreading out and stretching," said Prince Andrew to himself. While listening to this whispering and feeling the sensation of drawing out and the construction of this needle-like edifice, he also saw by glimpses a red halo around the candle, and heard the rustle of the cockroaches and the buzzing of the fly that bumped against his pillow and face. Each time the fly touched his face it gave him a burning sensation, and yet to his surprise it did not destroy the structure, though it hit the very spot where it was rising. But besides all this there was something else of importance. It was something white by the door—the statue of a sphinx, which also oppressed him.

261.20.oldText: "But perhaps that's my shirt on the table," he thought, "and those are my legs, and that is the door, but why is it always stretching and drawing itself out, and 'piti-piti-piti' and 'ti-ti' and 'piti-piti-piti'...? That's enough, please stop!" Prince Andrew painfully entreated someone. And suddenly thoughts and feelings again surfaced in his mind with peculiar clarity and force.

261.21.oldText: "Yes—love," he thought again quite clearly. "But not love that loves for something, for some quality, for some purpose, or for some reason, but the love which I—while dying—first experienced when I saw my enemy and yet loved him. I experienced that feeling of love which is the very essence of the soul and does not require an object. Now again I feel that bliss. To love one's neighbors, to love one's enemies, to love everything—to love God in all His forms. It is possible to love someone dear to you with human love, but an enemy can only be loved by divine love. That is why I experienced such joy when I felt that I loved that man. What has become of him? Is he alive?...

261.22.oldText: "When loving with human love one may pass from love to hatred, but divine love cannot change. No, neither death nor anything else can destroy it. It is the very essence of the soul. Yet how many people have I hated in my life? And of them all, I loved and hated none as I did her." And he vividly pictured Natasha to himself, not as he had done in the past with nothing but her charms which gave him pleasure, but for the first time picturing her soul. And he understood her feelings, her suffering, her shame, and her remorse. He now understood for the first time all the cruelty of his rejection of her, the cruelty of his break with her. "If only it were possible to see her once more! Just once, looking into those eyes to say..."

261.23.oldText: "Piti-piti-piti and ti-ti and piti-piti-piti boom!" buzzed the fly... And his attention was suddenly carried into another world, a world of reality and delirium in which something was happening. In that world some structure was still being built and did not fall, something was still stretching out, and the candle with its red halo was still burning, and the same shirt-like sphinx lay near the door; but besides all this something creaked, there was a breath of fresh air, and a new white sphinx appeared, standing at the door. And that sphinx had the pale face and shining eyes of the very Natasha of whom he had just been thinking.

261.24.oldText: "Oh, how oppressive this constant delirium is," thought Prince Andrew, trying to drive that face from his imagination. But the face remained before him with the force of reality and drew nearer. Prince Andrew wished to return to that former world of pure thought, but he could not, and delirium drew him back. The soft whispering voice continued its rhythmic murmur, something pressed on him and stretched out, and the strange face was before him. Prince Andrew gathered all his strength in an effort to recover his senses; he moved a little, and suddenly there was a ringing in his ears, a dimness in his eyes, and like a man plunged into water he lost consciousness. When he came to himself, Natasha—that same living Natasha whom of all people he most longed to love with this new, pure, divine love that had been revealed to him—was kneeling before him. He realized it was the real, living Natasha, and he was not surprised but quietly happy. Natasha, motionless on her knees (she could not move), with frightened eyes fixed on him, was holding back her sobs. Her face was pale and rigid. Only in the lower part of it something quivered.

261.25.oldText: Prince Andrew sighed with relief, smiled, and held out his hand.

261.27.oldText: With a quick but careful movement, Natasha drew closer to him on her knees and, taking his hand gently, bent her face over it and began kissing it, barely touching it with her lips.

261.32.oldText: "Forgive me for what I ha-ve do-ne!" Natasha faltered in a scarcely audible, broken whisper, and began kissing his hand more quickly, just touching it with her lips.

261.33.oldText: "I love you more, better than before," said Prince Andrew, lifting her face with his hand so he could look into her eyes.

261.34.oldText: Those eyes, filled with happy tears, gazed at him shyly, compassionately, and with joyous love. Natasha's thin pale face, with its swollen lips, was more than plain—it was awful. But Prince Andrew did not see that; he saw her shining eyes, which were beautiful. They heard the sound of voices behind them.

261.35.oldText: Peter the valet, now wide awake, had roused the doctor. Timokhin, who had not slept at all because of the pain in his leg, had long been watching everything, carefully covering his bare body with the sheet as he huddled on his bench.

261.36.oldText: "What's this?" said the doctor, rising from his bed. "Please go away, madam!"

261.37.oldText: At that moment a maid sent by the countess, who had noticed her daughter's absence, knocked at the door.

261.38.oldText: Like a sleepwalker awakened from her sleep, Natasha went out of the room and, returning to her hut, fell sobbing on her bed.

261.39.oldText: From that time on, during all the rest of the Rostovs' journey, at every stop and wherever they spent a night, Natasha never left the wounded Bolkonsky, and the doctor had to admit that he had not expected such firmness or such skill in nursing from a young girl.

261.40.oldText: Dreadful as the countess imagined it would be should Prince Andrew die in her daughter's arms during the journey—as, judging by what the doctor said, seemed possible—she could not oppose Natasha. Though with the intimacy now established between the wounded man and Natasha the thought occurred that should he recover their former engagement would be renewed, no one—least of all Natasha and Prince Andrew—spoke of this. The unsettled question of life and death, which hung not only over Bolkonsky but over all Russia, shut out every other consideration.

263.0.oldText: Having run through various yards and side streets, Pierre got back with his little burden to the Gruzinsky garden at the corner of the Povarskoy. He did not at first recognize the place from which he had set out to look for the child, so crowded was it now with people and goods that had been dragged out of the houses. Besides Russian families who had taken refuge here from the fire with their belongings, there were several French soldiers in various clothing. Pierre took no notice of them. He hurried to find the family of that civil servant in order to return the daughter to her mother and go save someone else. Pierre felt that he still had much to do and had to do it quickly. Glowing with the heat and from running, he felt at that moment more strongly than ever the sense of youth, energy, and determination that had come over him when he ran to save the child. She had now become quiet and, clinging with her little hands to Pierre's coat, sat on his arm gazing about her like some little wild animal. He glanced at her occasionally with a slight smile. He thought he saw something touchingly innocent in that frightened, sickly little face.

263.1.oldText: He did not find the civil servant or his wife where he had left them. He walked among the crowd with quick steps, scanning the various faces. Involuntarily he noticed a Georgian or Armenian family consisting of a very handsome old man of Eastern appearance wearing a new cloth-covered sheepskin coat and new boots, an old woman of similar type, and a young woman. That very young woman seemed to Pierre the perfection of Eastern beauty, with her sharply arched black eyebrows and the extraordinarily soft, bright color of her long, beautiful, expressionless face. Amid the scattered property and the crowd in the open space, she, in her rich satin cloak with a bright lilac shawl on her head, suggested a delicate exotic plant thrown onto the snow. She was sitting on some bundles a little behind the old woman, and looked from under her long lashes with motionless, large, almond-shaped eyes at the ground before her. Evidently she was aware of her beauty and fearful because of it. Her face struck Pierre, and hurrying along by the fence, he turned several times to look at her. When he had reached the fence, still without finding those he sought, he stopped and looked about him.

263.2.oldText: With the child in his arms, his figure was now more noticeable, and a group of Russians—both men and women—gathered around him.

263.3.oldText: "Have you lost someone, my dear fellow? You're a gentleman yourself, aren't you? Whose child is it?" they asked him.

263.4.oldText: Pierre replied that the child belonged to a woman in a black coat who had been sitting there with her other children, and he asked whether anyone knew where she had gone.

263.5.oldText: "Why, that must be the Anferovs," said an old deacon, addressing a pockmarked peasant woman. "Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy!" he added in his customary bass.

263.6.oldText: "The Anferovs? No," said the woman. "They left in the morning. That must be either Maria Nikolaevna's or the Ivanovs'!"

263.7.oldText: "He says 'a woman,' and Maria Nikolaevna is a lady," remarked a house servant.

263.9.oldText: "That's Maria Nikolaevna! They went into the garden when these wolves swooped down," said the woman, pointing to the French soldiers.

263.11.oldText: "Go over that way, they're there. It's her! She kept crying and carrying on," continued the woman. "It's her. Here, this way!"

263.12.oldText: But Pierre was not listening to the woman. He had for some seconds been intently watching what was happening a few steps away. He was looking at the Armenian family and at two French soldiers who had gone up to them. One of them, a quick little man, was wearing a blue coat tied round the waist with a rope. He had a nightcap on his head and his feet were bare. The other, whose appearance particularly struck Pierre, was a tall, lanky, round-shouldered, fair-haired man, slow in his movements and with a vacant expression. He wore a woman's loose gown of rough cloth, blue trousers, and large torn Hessian boots. The little barefooted Frenchman in the blue coat went up to the Armenians and, saying something, immediately seized the old man by his legs and the old man began pulling off his boots. The other, in the rough cloth gown, stopped in front of the beautiful Armenian girl and, with his hands in his pockets, stood staring at her, motionless and silent.

263.13.oldText: "Here, take the child!" said Pierre urgently and hurriedly to the woman, handing the little girl to her. "Give her back to them, give her back!" he almost shouted, putting the screaming child on the ground, and turning back to look at the Frenchman and the Armenian family.

263.14.oldText: The old man was already sitting barefoot. The little Frenchman had secured his second boot and was slapping one boot against the other. The old man was saying something in a voice broken by sobs, but Pierre caught only a glimpse of this—his whole attention was on the Frenchman in the rough gown, who meanwhile, swaying slowly from side to side, had drawn nearer to the young woman and, taking his hands from his pockets, had seized her by the neck.

263.15.oldText: The beautiful Armenian still sat motionless and in the same position, with her long lashes drooping as if she did not see or feel what the soldier was doing to her.

263.16.oldText: While Pierre was running the few steps that separated him from the Frenchman, the tall marauder in the rough gown was already tearing the necklace from the young Armenian woman's neck, and the young woman, clutching at her throat, screamed piercingly.

263.17.oldText: "Leave that woman alone!" Pierre exclaimed hoarsely in a furious voice, seizing the soldier by his round shoulders and throwing him aside.

263.18.oldText: The soldier fell, got up, and ran away. But his comrade, dropping the boots and drawing his sword, moved threateningly toward Pierre.

263.21.oldText: Pierre was in such a transport of rage that he remembered nothing, and his strength increased tenfold. He rushed at the barefooted Frenchman and, before the latter could draw his sword, knocked him off his feet and hammered him with his fists. Shouts of approval were heard from the crowd around, and at the same moment a mounted patrol of French Uhlans appeared from around the corner. The Uhlans came up at a trot to Pierre and the Frenchman and surrounded them. Pierre remembered nothing of what happened after that. He only remembered beating someone and being beaten, and finally feeling that his hands were bound and that a crowd of French soldiers stood around him, searching him.

263.23.oldText: "Ah, a weapon?" said the officer, and turned to the barefooted soldier who had been arrested with Pierre. "All right, you can tell all about it at the court-martial." Then he turned to Pierre. "Do you speak French?"

263.24.oldText: Pierre looked around him with bloodshot eyes and did not reply. His face probably looked very terrible, for the officer said something in a whisper and four more Uhlans left the ranks and positioned themselves on both sides of Pierre.

263.25.oldText: "Do you speak French?" the officer asked again, keeping his distance from Pierre. "Call the interpreter."

263.26.oldText: A small man in Russian civilian clothes rode out from the ranks, and by his clothes and manner of speaking Pierre at once recognized him as a French salesman from one of the Moscow shops.

263.27.oldText: "He doesn't look like a common man," said the interpreter, after giving Pierre a searching look.

263.28.oldText: "Ah, he looks very much like an arsonist," remarked the officer. "And ask him who he is," he added.

263.30.oldText: "I will not tell you who I am. I am your prisoner—take me!" Pierre suddenly replied in French.

263.31.oldText: "Ah, ah!" muttered the officer with a frown. "Well then, march!"

263.32.oldText: A crowd had gathered around the Uhlans. Nearest to Pierre stood the pockmarked peasant woman with the little girl, and when the patrol started she moved forward.

263.33.oldText: "Where are they taking you, you poor dear?" said she. "And the little girl, the little girl—what am I supposed to do with her if she's not theirs?" said the woman.

263.35.oldText: Pierre was as if intoxicated. His exhilaration increased at the sight of the little girl he had saved.

263.36.oldText: "What does she want?" he murmured. "She is bringing me my daughter whom I have just saved from the flames," said he. "Goodbye!" And without knowing how this pointless lie had escaped him, he walked on with resolute, triumphant steps between the French soldiers.

263.37.oldText: The French patrol was one of those sent out through the various streets of Moscow by Durosnel's order to put a stop to the pillaging, and especially to catch the arsonists who, according to the prevailing opinion among the higher French officers, were the cause of the fires. After marching through a number of streets, the patrol arrested five more Russian suspects: a small shopkeeper, two seminary students, a peasant, and a house servant, besides several looters. But of all these various suspected characters, Pierre was considered the most suspicious of all. When they had all been brought for the night to a large house on the Zubov Rampart that was being used as a guardhouse, Pierre was placed apart under strict guard.

265.0.oldText: Anna Pavlovna's premonition was in fact fulfilled. Next day during the service at the palace church in honor of the Emperor's birthday, Prince Volkonsky was called out of the church and received a dispatch from Prince Kutuzov. It was Kutuzov's report, written from Tatarinova on the day of the battle. Kutuzov wrote that the Russians had not retreated a step, that the French losses were much heavier than theirs, and that he was writing in haste from the field of battle before collecting full information. It followed that there must have been a victory. And at once, without leaving the church, thanks were given to the Creator for His help and for the victory.

265.1.oldText: Anna Pavlovna's premonition was justified, and all that morning a joyously festive mood reigned in the city. Everyone believed the victory to have been complete, and some even spoke of Napoleon's capture, his removal from power, and the selection of a new ruler for France.

265.2.oldText: It is very difficult for events to be reflected in their true magnitude amid the conditions of court life and far from the scene of action. General events inevitably cluster around some particular incident. So now the courtiers' pleasure was based as much on the fact that the news arrived on the Emperor's birthday as on the fact of the victory itself. It was like a perfectly arranged surprise. In Kutuzov's report, the Russian losses were mentioned, including the names of Tuchkov, Bagration, and Kutaysov. In the Petersburg world, this sad aspect of the affair again instinctively centered around a single incident: the death of Kutaysov. Everybody knew him, the Emperor liked him, and he was young and interesting. That day everyone greeted each other with the words:

265.4.oldText: "What did I tell you about Kutuzov?" Prince Vasili now said with a prophet's pride. "I always said he was the only man capable of defeating Napoleon."

265.5.oldText: But the next day no news arrived from the army, and the public mood grew anxious. The courtiers suffered because of the suffering the suspense caused the Emperor.

265.6.oldText: "Imagine the Emperor's position!" they said, and instead of praising Kutuzov as they had the day before, they condemned him as the cause of the Emperor's anxiety. That day Prince Vasili no longer boasted of his protege Kutuzov but remained silent when the commander in chief was mentioned. Moreover, toward evening, as if everything conspired to make Petersburg society anxious and uneasy, terrible news arrived. Countess Helene Bezukhova had suddenly died of that terrible malady it had been so agreeable to mention. Officially, at large gatherings, everyone said that Countess Bezukhova had died of a terrible attack of angina pectoris, but in intimate circles details were mentioned of how the Queen of Spain's private physician had prescribed small doses of a certain drug to produce a certain effect; but Helene, tormented by the fact that the old count suspected her and that her husband—to whom she had written (that wretched, dissolute Pierre)—had not replied, had suddenly taken a very large dose of the drug and had died in agony before help could be given. It was said that Prince Vasili and the old count had turned on the Italian, but the latter produced letters from the unfortunate deceased that made them immediately drop the matter.

265.7.oldText: Talk in general centered around three melancholy facts: the Emperor's lack of news, the loss of Kutaysov, and the death of Helene.

265.8.oldText: On the third day after Kutuzov's report, a country gentleman arrived from Moscow, and news of the surrender of Moscow to the French spread through the whole town. This was terrible! What a position for the Emperor to be in! Kutuzov was a traitor, and Prince Vasili, during the condolence visits paid to him on the occasion of his daughter's death, said of Kutuzov—whom he had formerly praised (it was excusable for him in his grief to forget what he had said)—that nothing else could be expected from a blind and depraved old man.

265.10.oldText: As long as this news remained unofficial it was possible to doubt it, but the next day the following communication was received from Count Rostopchin:

265.11.oldText: Prince Kutuzov's adjutant has brought me a letter in which he demands police officers to guide the army to the Ryazan road. He writes that he is regretfully abandoning Moscow. Sire! Kutuzov's action decides the fate of the capital and of your empire! Russia will shudder to learn of the abandonment of the city in which her greatness is centered and in which lie the ashes of your ancestors! I shall follow the army. I have had everything removed, and it only remains for me to weep over the fate of my fatherland.

265.12.oldText: On receiving this dispatch the Emperor sent Prince Volkonsky to Kutuzov with the following message:

265.13.oldText: Prince Michael Ilarionovich! Since the twenty-ninth of August I have received no communication from you, yet on the first of September I received from the commander in chief of Moscow, via Yaroslavl, the sad news that you, with the army, have decided to abandon Moscow. You can yourself imagine the effect this news has had on me, and your silence increases my astonishment. I am sending this by Adjutant-General Prince Volkonsky, to hear from you the situation of the army and the reasons that have induced you to take this melancholy decision.

266.0.oldText: Nine days after the abandonment of Moscow, a messenger from Kutuzov reached Petersburg with the official announcement of that event. This messenger was Michaud, a Frenchman who did not know Russian, but who was, as he said of himself, "though a foreigner, Russian in heart and soul."

266.2.oldText: The Emperor at once received this messenger in his study at the palace on Stone Island. Michaud, who had never seen Moscow before the campaign and who did not know Russian, was nevertheless deeply moved (as he wrote) when he appeared before "our most gracious sovereign" with the news of the burning of Moscow, "whose flames illumined his route."

266.5.oldText: Though the source of Monsieur Michaud's distress must have been different from that which caused Russians to grieve, he had such a sad face when shown into the Emperor's study that the latter at once asked:

266.6.oldText: "Have you brought me sad news, Colonel?"

266.7.oldText: "Very sad, sire," replied Michaud, lowering his eyes with a sigh. "The abandonment of Moscow."

266.8.oldText: "Have they surrendered my ancient capital without a battle?" asked the Emperor quickly, his face suddenly flushing.

266.9.oldText: Michaud respectfully delivered the message Kutuzov had entrusted to him: that it had been impossible to fight before Moscow, and that since the only remaining choice was between losing the army as well as Moscow or losing Moscow alone, the field marshal had chosen the latter.

266.10.oldText: The Emperor listened in silence, not looking at Michaud.

266.12.oldText: "Yes, sire, and Moscow is now in ashes. I left it all in flames," replied Michaud in a firm tone, but glancing at the Emperor he was frightened by what he had done.

266.13.oldText: The Emperor began to breathe heavily and rapidly, his lower lip trembled, and tears instantly appeared in his fine blue eyes.

266.14.oldText: But this lasted only a moment. He suddenly frowned, as if blaming himself for his weakness, and raising his head addressed Michaud in a firm voice:

266.15.oldText: "I see, Colonel, from all that is happening, that Providence requires great sacrifices of us... I am ready to submit myself in all things to His will; but tell me, Michaud, how did you leave the army when it saw my ancient capital abandoned without a battle? Did you not notice discouragement?..."

266.16.oldText: Seeing that his most gracious ruler was calm once more, Michaud also grew calm, but was not immediately ready to reply to the Emperor's direct and relevant question, which required a direct answer.

266.17.oldText: "Sire, will you allow me to speak frankly as befits a loyal soldier?" he asked, to gain time.

266.18.oldText: "Colonel, I always require it," replied the Emperor. "Conceal nothing from me. I wish to know absolutely how things are."

266.19.oldText: "Sire!" said Michaud with a subtle, barely perceptible smile on his lips, having now prepared a well-phrased reply, "sire, I left the whole army, from its chiefs to the lowest soldier, without exception, in desperate and agonized terror..."

266.20.oldText: "How is that?" the Emperor interrupted him, frowning sternly. "Would misfortune make my Russians lose heart?... Never!"

266.21.oldText: Michaud had only waited for this to deliver the phrase he had prepared.

266.22.oldText: "Sire," he said, with respectful playfulness, "they are only afraid that Your Majesty, in the goodness of your heart, might allow yourself to be persuaded to make peace. They are burning for combat," declared this representative of the Russian nation, "and eager to prove to Your Majesty by the sacrifice of their lives how devoted they are..."

266.23.oldText: "Ah!" said the Emperor reassured, and with a kindly gleam in his eyes, he patted Michaud on the shoulder. "You set me at ease, Colonel."

266.24.oldText: He bowed his head and was silent for some time.

266.25.oldText: "Well, then, go back to the army," he said, drawing himself up to his full height and addressing Michaud with a gracious and majestic gesture, "and tell our brave men and all my good subjects wherever you go that when I have not a soldier left I shall put myself at the head of my beloved nobility and my good peasants, and so use the last resources of my empire. It still offers me more than my enemies suppose," said the Emperor, growing more and more animated. "But should it ever be ordained by Divine Providence," he continued, raising to heaven his fine eyes shining with emotion, "that my dynasty should cease to reign on the throne of my ancestors, then after exhausting all the means at my command, I shall let my beard grow to here" (he pointed halfway down his chest) "and go and eat potatoes with the meanest of my peasants, rather than sign the disgrace of my country and of my beloved people whose sacrifices I know how to value."

266.26.oldText: Having uttered these words in an agitated voice, the Emperor suddenly turned away as if to hide from Michaud the tears that rose to his eyes, and went to the far end of his study. Having stood there a few moments, he strode back to Michaud and pressed his arm below the elbow with a vigorous movement. The Emperor's mild, handsome face was flushed and his eyes gleamed with resolution and anger.

266.27.oldText: "Colonel Michaud, do not forget what I say to you here; perhaps we may recall it with pleasure someday... Napoleon or I," said the Emperor, touching his chest. "We can no longer both reign together. I have learned to know him, and he will not deceive me any more..."

266.28.oldText: And the Emperor paused, with a frown.

266.29.oldText: When he heard these words and saw the expression of firm resolution in the Emperor's eyes, Michaud—though a foreigner, Russian in heart and soul—felt himself at that solemn moment enraptured by all that he had heard (as he afterwards used to say), and gave expression to his own feelings and those of the Russian people, whose representative he considered himself to be, in the following words:

266.30.oldText: "Sire!" said he, "Your Majesty is at this moment signing the glory of the nation and the salvation of Europe!"

266.31.oldText: With a nod, the Emperor dismissed him.

267.0.oldText: It is natural for us who did not live in those days to imagine that when half of Russia had been conquered and the inhabitants were fleeing to distant provinces, and one levy after another was being raised for the defense of the fatherland, all Russians from greatest to least were solely engaged in sacrificing themselves, saving their fatherland, or weeping over its downfall. The tales and descriptions of that time without exception speak only of the self-sacrifice, patriotic devotion, despair, grief, and heroism of the Russians. But it was not really so. It appears so to us because we see only the general historical interest of that time and do not see all the personal human interests that people had. Yet in reality those personal interests of the moment so far outweighed the general interests that they always prevented the public interest from being felt or even noticed. Most of the people at that time paid no attention to the general course of events but were guided only by their private interests, and they were precisely the people whose activities in that period were most useful.

267.1.oldText: Those who tried to understand the general course of events and take part in it through self-sacrifice and heroism were the most useless members of society; they saw everything backward, and all they did for the common good turned out to be useless and foolish—like Pierre's and Mamonov's regiments which looted Russian villages, or the bandages the young ladies prepared that never reached the wounded, and so on. Even those who were fond of intellectual talk and of expressing their feelings, who discussed Russia's position at the time, involuntarily introduced into their conversations either a shade of pretense and falsehood or useless condemnation and anger directed against people accused of actions no one could possibly be guilty of. In historic events, the rule forbidding us to eat of the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge is especially applicable. Only unconscious action bears fruit, and the person who plays a part in a historic event never understands its significance. If he tries to understand it, his efforts are fruitless.

267.2.oldText: The more closely a person was involved in the events taking place in Russia, the less did he understand their significance. In Petersburg and in the provinces far from Moscow, ladies and gentlemen in militia uniforms wept for Russia and its ancient capital and talked of self-sacrifice and so on; but in the army, which had retreated beyond Moscow, there was little talk or thought of Moscow, and when they caught sight of its burned ruins no one swore to be avenged on the French. Instead they thought about their next pay, their next quarters, about Matreshka the canteen woman, and similar matters.

267.3.oldText: Since the war had caught him in the service, Nicholas Rostov took a close and prolonged part in the defense of his country, but did so casually, without any aim at self-sacrifice, and he therefore looked at what was going on in Russia without despair and without racking his brains over it. Had he been asked what he thought of the state of Russia, he would have said it was not his business to think about it, that Kutuzov and others were there for that, but that he had heard the regiments were being brought up to full strength, that fighting would probably go on for a long time yet, and that given how things were, he might quite possibly be commanding a regiment in a couple of years.

267.4.oldText: Viewing the situation this way, he learned that he was being sent to Voronezh to buy replacement horses for his division—not only without regret at missing the coming battle, but with the greatest pleasure, which he made no attempt to hide and which his comrades fully understood.

267.5.oldText: A few days before the battle of Borodino, Nicholas received the necessary money and warrants and, having sent some hussars on ahead, set out with post horses for Voronezh.

267.6.oldText: Only a man who has experienced it—that is, has spent several months continuously in the atmosphere of campaigning and war—can understand the delight Nicholas felt when he escaped from the region covered by the army's foraging operations, supply trains, and hospitals. When—free from soldiers, wagons, and the filthy traces of a camp—he saw villages with peasants and peasant women, gentlemen's country houses, fields with grazing cattle, and post stations with stationmasters asleep in them, he rejoiced as though seeing all this for the first time. What especially surprised and delighted him for a long time were the women—young and healthy, without a dozen officers flirting with each of them; women, too, who were pleased and flattered that a passing officer should joke with them.

267.7.oldText: In the highest spirits, Nicholas arrived at a hotel in Voronezh at night, ordered things he had long been deprived of in camp, and next day, very cleanly shaved and in a full-dress uniform he had not worn for a long time, went to present himself to the authorities.

267.8.oldText: The commander of the militia was a civilian general, an old man who was obviously pleased with his military title and rank. He received Nicholas brusquely (imagining this to be characteristically military) and questioned him with an important air, as if considering the general progress of affairs and approving or disapproving with full right to do so. Nicholas was in such good spirits that this merely amused him.

267.9.oldText: From the militia commander he drove to the governor. The governor was a brisk little man, very simple and friendly. He pointed out the stud farms where Nicholas might find horses, recommended a horse dealer in the town and a landowner fourteen miles away who had the best horses, and promised to help in every way.

267.10.oldText: "You are Count Ilya Rostov's son? My wife was a great friend of your mother's. We are at home on Thursdays—today is Thursday, so please come and see us informally," said the governor, taking leave of him.

267.11.oldText: Immediately on leaving the governor's, Nicholas hired post horses and, taking his squadron quartermaster with him, drove at a gallop to the landowner fourteen miles away who had the stud. Everything seemed pleasant and easy during that first part of his stay in Voronezh, and as usually happens when a man is in a good mood, everything went well and smoothly.

267.12.oldText: The landowner Nicholas went to was a bachelor, an old cavalryman, a horse lover, a sportsman, the owner of some century-old brandy and some old Hungarian wine, who had a cozy den where he smoked, and who possessed some splendid horses.

267.13.oldText: In very few words Nicholas bought seventeen picked stallions for six thousand rubles—to serve, as he said, as samples of his remounts. After dining and drinking rather too much of the Hungarian wine, Nicholas—having exchanged kisses with the landowner, with whom he was already on the friendliest terms—galloped back over terrible roads in the brightest frame of mind, constantly urging on the driver so as to be in time for the governor's party.

267.14.oldText: When he had changed, poured water over his head, and applied cologne, Nicholas arrived at the governor's rather late, but with the phrase "better late than never" on his lips.

267.15.oldText: It was not a ball, nor had dancing been announced, but everyone knew that Catherine Petrovna would play waltzes and the ecossaise on the clavichord and that there would be dancing, and so everyone had come as to a ball.

267.16.oldText: Provincial life in 1812 went on much as usual, but with one difference: it was livelier in the towns because of the arrival of many wealthy families from Moscow, and as in everything that went on in Russia at that time, a special recklessness was noticeable—an "in for a penny, in for a pound—who cares?" spirit—and the inevitable small talk, instead of turning on the weather and mutual acquaintances, now turned on Moscow, the army, and Napoleon.

267.18.oldText: There were a great many ladies and some of Nicholas's Moscow acquaintances, but there were no men who could at all compete with the cavalier of St. George, the hussar remount officer, the good-natured and well-bred Count Rostov. Among the men was an Italian prisoner, an officer of the French army; and Nicholas felt that the presence of this prisoner enhanced his own importance as a Russian hero. The Italian was, as it were, a war trophy. Nicholas felt this; it seemed to him that everyone regarded the Italian the same way, and he treated him with gracious dignity and restraint.

267.19.oldText: As soon as Nicholas entered in his hussar uniform, spreading around him a fragrance of perfume and wine, and had uttered the words "better late than never" and heard them repeated several times by others, people clustered around him; all eyes turned on him, and he felt at once that he had entered his proper position in the province—that of a universal favorite: a very pleasant position, and intoxicatingly so after his long privations. At posting stations, at inns, and in the landowner's cozy den, maidservants had been flattered by his notice, and here too at the governor's party there were (as it seemed to Nicholas) an inexhaustible number of pretty young women, married and unmarried, eagerly awaiting his attention. The women and girls flirted with him, and from the very first day, the people around them set about trying to get this fine young daredevil of a hussar married and settled down. Among these was the governor's wife herself, who welcomed Rostov as a close relative and called him "Nicholas."

267.20.oldText: Catherine Petrovna did play waltzes and the ecossaise, and dancing began in which Nicholas further captivated provincial society with his agility. His particularly free and easy manner of dancing even surprised them all. Nicholas was himself rather surprised at how he danced that evening. He had never danced like that in Moscow and would even have considered such a very free and easy manner improper and in bad form there, but here he felt it was his duty to astonish them all with something unusual, something they would have to accept as the standard in the capital, though new to them in the provinces.

267.21.oldText: All evening Nicholas paid attention to a blue-eyed, plump and pleasing little blonde, the wife of one of the provincial officials. With the naive conviction of young men in a merry mood that other men's wives were created for them, Rostov did not leave the lady's side and treated her husband in a friendly and conspiratorial manner, as if, without saying so, they both knew how perfectly Nicholas and the lady would get along. The husband, however, did not seem to share that conviction and tried to behave coldly toward Rostov. But Nicholas's good-natured openness was so boundless that sometimes even the husband involuntarily yielded to his good humor. Toward the end of the evening, however, as the wife's face grew more flushed and animated, the husband's became more and more gloomy and solemn, as though there were a fixed amount of animation between them—and as the wife's share increased, the husband's diminished.

269.0.oldText: On reaching Moscow after her meeting with Rostov, Princess Mary had found her nephew there with his tutor, and a letter from Prince Andrew giving her instructions on how to reach her Aunt Malvintseva in Voronezh. That feeling akin to temptation which had tormented her during her father's illness, since his death, and especially since her meeting with Rostov, was smothered by the arrangements for the journey, anxiety about her brother, settling in a new house, meeting new people, and attending to her nephew's education. She was sad. Now, after a month in quiet surroundings, she felt more and more deeply the loss of her father—a loss associated in her mind with the ruin of Russia. She was agitated and constantly tortured by the thought of the dangers threatening her brother, the only close person now remaining to her. She worried too about her nephew's education, for which she had always felt herself inadequate. But in the depths of her soul she felt at peace—a peace arising from the knowledge that she had suppressed those personal dreams and hopes that had been on the point of awakening within her, connected to her meeting with Rostov.

269.1.oldText: The day after her party, the governor's wife came to see Malvintseva, and after discussing her plan with the aunt, remarked that though under present circumstances a formal engagement was of course out of the question, the young people might still be brought together and could get to know one another. Malvintseva expressed approval, and the governor's wife began to speak of Rostov in Mary's presence, praising him and telling how he had blushed when Princess Mary's name was mentioned. But Princess Mary experienced a painful rather than joyful feeling—her mental peace was destroyed, and desires, doubts, self-reproach, and hopes reawakened.

269.2.oldText: During the two days before Rostov called, Princess Mary continually thought about how she ought to behave toward him.
