First she decided not to come to the drawing room when he called to see her aunt—that it would not be proper for her, in her deep mourning, to receive visitors; then she thought this would be rude after what he had done for her; then it occurred to her that her aunt and the governor's wife had intentions concerning her and Rostov—their looks and words sometimes seemed to confirm this suspicion—then she told herself that only she, with her sinful nature, could think this of them: they could not forget that in her position, while still wearing deep mourning, such matchmaking would be an insult to her and to her father's memory. Assuming she did go down to see him, Princess Mary imagined the words he would say to her and what she would say to him, and these words sometimes seemed undeservedly cold and then too full of meaning. More than anything she feared that the confusion she felt might overwhelm her and betray her as soon as she saw him.

269.3.oldText: But when on Sunday after church the footman announced in the drawing room that Count Rostov had called, the princess showed no confusion. Only a slight blush came to her cheeks and her eyes lit up with a new and radiant light.

269.4.oldText: "You have met him, Aunt?" said she in a calm voice, unable herself to understand how she could be so outwardly calm and natural.

269.5.oldText: When Rostov entered the room, the princess dropped her eyes for an instant, as if to give the visitor time to greet her aunt, and then, just as Nicholas turned to her, she raised her head and met his gaze with shining eyes. With a movement full of dignity and grace she half rose with a smile of pleasure, held out her slender, delicate hand, and began to speak in a voice in which, for the first time, new deep womanly notes vibrated. Mademoiselle Bourienne, who was in the drawing room, looked at Princess Mary in bewildered surprise. A consummate flirt herself, she could not have maneuvered better on meeting a man she wished to attract.

269.6.oldText: "Either black is particularly becoming to her, or she really has greatly improved without my noticing it. And above all, what tact and grace!" thought Mademoiselle Bourienne.

269.7.oldText: Had Princess Mary been capable of reflection at that moment, she would have been more surprised than Mademoiselle Bourienne at the change in herself. From the moment she recognized that dear, loved face, a new life force took possession of her and compelled her to speak and act apart from her own will. From the moment Rostov entered, her face was suddenly transformed. It was as if a light had been kindled in a carved and painted lantern, and the intricate, skillful, artistic work on its sides—that previously seemed dark, coarse, and meaningless—was suddenly revealed in unexpected and striking beauty. For the first time, all that pure, spiritual, inward labor through which she had lived appeared on the surface. All her inner work, her dissatisfaction with herself, her suffering, her striving for goodness, her gentleness, love, and self-sacrifice—all this now shone in those radiant eyes, in her delicate smile, and in every feature of her gentle face.

269.8.oldText: Rostov saw all this as clearly as if he had known her his whole life. He felt that the person before him was quite different from, and better than, anyone he had met before, and above all better than himself.

269.9.oldText: Their conversation was very simple and unimportant. They spoke of the war, and like everyone else unconsciously exaggerated their sorrow about it; they spoke of their last meeting—Nicholas trying to change the subject—they talked of the governor's kind wife, of Nicholas's relatives, and of Princess Mary's.

269.10.oldText: She did not talk about her brother, steering the conversation away as soon as her aunt mentioned Andrew. Evidently she could speak of Russia's misfortunes with a certain artificiality, but her brother was too close to her heart and she neither could nor would speak lightly of him. Nicholas noticed this, as he noticed every shade of Princess Mary's character with an observation unusual for him, and everything confirmed his conviction that she was a quite unusual and extraordinary person. Nicholas blushed and grew confused when people spoke to him about the princess (as she did when he was mentioned) and even when he thought of her, but in her presence he felt completely at ease and said not at all what he had prepared, but what, quite naturally, occurred to him at the moment.

269.11.oldText: When a pause occurred during his short visit, Nicholas, as is usual when there are children, turned to Prince Andrew's little son, caressing him and asking whether he would like to be a hussar. He took the boy on his knee, played with him, and looked over at Princess Mary. With a softened, happy, shy look she watched the boy she loved in the arms of the man she loved. Nicholas also noticed that look and, as if understanding it, flushed with pleasure and began kissing the boy with good-natured playfulness.

269.12.oldText: As she was in mourning, Princess Mary did not go out in society, and Nicholas did not think it proper to visit her again; but the governor's wife continued her matchmaking, passing on to Nicholas the flattering things Princess Mary said about him and vice versa, and insisting that he declare himself to Princess Mary. For this purpose she arranged a meeting between the young people at the bishop's house before Mass.

269.13.oldText: Though Rostov told the governor's wife that he would make no declaration to Princess Mary, he promised to go.

269.14.oldText: Just as at Tilsit Rostov had not allowed himself to doubt that what everybody considered right was right, so now, after a short but sincere struggle between his effort to arrange his life according to his own sense of justice and his obedient submission to circumstances, he chose the latter and yielded to the power that he felt irresistibly carrying him he knew not where. He knew that after his promise to Sonya it would be what he considered dishonorable to declare his feelings to Princess Mary. And he knew that he would never act dishonorably. But he also knew (or rather felt at the bottom of his heart) that by yielding now to the force of circumstances and to those who were guiding him, he was not only doing nothing wrong but was doing something very important—more important than anything he had ever done in his life.

269.15.oldText: After meeting Princess Mary, though his daily routine went on as before, all his former amusements lost their charm and he often thought about her. But he never thought about her as he had thought of all the young ladies he had met in society without exception, nor as he had for a long time—and at one point rapturously—thought about Sonya. He had pictured each of those young ladies as almost all honest-hearted young men do, that is, as a possible wife, fitting her in his imagination to all the conditions of married life: a white dressing gown, his wife at the tea table, his wife's carriage, little ones, Mama and Papa, their relations to her, and so on—and these pictures of the future had given him pleasure. But with Princess Mary, to whom they were trying to get him engaged, he could never picture anything of future married life. If he tried, his pictures seemed incongruous and false. It made him afraid.

270.0.oldText: The dreadful news of the battle of Borodino, of the losses in killed and wounded, and the still more terrible news of the fall of Moscow reached Voronezh in the middle of September. Princess Mary, having learned of her brother's wound only from the official gazette, and having no definite news of him, prepared (so Nicholas heard—he had not seen her again) to set off in search of Prince Andrew.

270.1.oldText: When he received the news of the battle of Borodino and the abandonment of Moscow, Rostov was not seized with despair, anger, the desire for vengeance, or any feeling of that kind. Instead, everything in Voronezh suddenly seemed dull and tiresome, and he felt an indefinite sense of shame and awkwardness. The conversations he heard seemed insincere; he did not know how to judge all these affairs and felt that only in the regiment would everything become clear again. He hurried to finish buying the horses and often became unreasonably angry with his servant and squadron quartermaster.

270.2.oldText: A few days before his departure, a special thanksgiving service was held in the cathedral for the Russian victory, and Nicholas was present. He stood a little behind the governor and held himself with military decorum throughout the service, meditating on a great variety of subjects. When the service was over the governor's wife beckoned him to her.

270.3.oldText: "Have you seen the princess?" she asked, indicating with a nod a lady standing on the opposite side, beyond the choir.

270.4.oldText: Nicholas immediately recognized Princess Mary—not so much by the profile he saw under her bonnet as by the feeling of concern, shyness, and pity that instantly overcame him. Princess Mary, evidently engrossed in her thoughts, was crossing herself for the last time before leaving the church.

270.5.oldText: Nicholas looked at her face with surprise. It was the same face he had seen before, with the same general expression of refined inner spiritual effort, but now it was quite differently lit up. There was a touching expression of sorrow, prayer, and hope in it. As had happened before when she was present, Nicholas went up to her without waiting for the governor's wife's prompting and without asking himself whether it was right and proper to address her here in church, and told her he had heard of her trouble and sympathized with his whole soul. As soon as she heard his voice, a vivid glow kindled in her face, lighting up both her sorrow and her joy.

270.6.oldText: "There is one thing I wanted to tell you, Princess," said Rostov. "It is that if your brother, Prince Andrew Nikolaevich, were not living, the news would have been announced in the gazette at once, since he is a colonel."

270.7.oldText: The princess looked at him, not grasping what he was saying, but cheered by the expression of regretful sympathy on his face.

270.8.oldText: "And I have known so many cases of a splinter wound" (the gazette said it was a shell) "either proving fatal at once or being very slight," continued Nicholas. "We must hope for the best, and I am sure..."

270.10.oldText: "Oh, that would be so dread..." she began and, prevented by emotion from finishing, bent her head with a movement as graceful as everything she did in his presence, and looking up at him gratefully, went out, following her aunt.

270.11.oldText: That evening Nicholas did not go out but stayed at home to settle some accounts with the horse dealers. When he had finished that business it was already too late to go anywhere but still too early for bed, and for a long time he paced up and down the room reflecting on his life—something he rarely did.

270.12.oldText: Princess Mary had made an agreeable impression on him when he had met her in Smolensk province. His having encountered her in such exceptional circumstances, and his mother's having at one time mentioned her as a good match, had drawn his particular attention to her. When he met her again in Voronezh, the impression she made on him was not merely pleasing but powerful. Nicholas had been struck by the peculiar moral beauty he observed in her at this time. He was, however, preparing to leave, and it had not entered his head to regret missing chances to see her. But that day's encounter in the church had, he felt, sunk deeper than was desirable for his peace of mind. That pale, sad, refined face, that radiant look, those gentle, graceful gestures, and especially the deep and tender sorrow expressed in all her features agitated him and stirred his sympathy. In men, Rostov could not bear to see the expression of a higher spiritual life (that was why he did not like Prince Andrew), and he referred to it dismissively as philosophy and dreaminess; but in Princess Mary, that very sorrow which revealed the depth of a whole spiritual world foreign to him was an irresistible attraction.

270.13.oldText: "She must be a wonderful woman. A real angel!" he said to himself. "Why am I not free? Why was I in such a hurry with Sonya?" And he involuntarily compared the two: the lack of spirituality in the one and the abundance of it in the other—a spirituality he himself lacked and therefore valued most highly. He tried to picture what would happen if he were free. How he would propose to her and how she would become his wife. But no, he could not imagine it. He felt awe, and no clear picture presented itself to his mind. He had long ago pictured a future with Sonya, and it was all clear and simple because it had all been thought out and he knew everything there was in Sonya. But it was impossible to picture a future with Princess Mary, because he did not understand her but simply loved her.

270.14.oldText: Daydreams about Sonya had something merry and playful in them, but to dream of Princess Mary was always difficult and a little frightening.

270.15.oldText: "How she prayed!" he thought. "It was plain that her whole soul was in her prayer. Yes, that was the prayer that moves mountains, and I am sure her prayer will be answered. Why don't I pray for what I want?" he suddenly thought. "What do I want? To be free, released from Sonya... She was right," he thought, remembering what the governor's wife had said: "Nothing but misfortune can come of marrying Sonya. Confusion, grief for Mama... business difficulties... confusion, terrible confusion! Besides, I don't love her—not as I should. O God! Release me from this dreadful, inextricable situation!" he suddenly began to pray. "Yes, prayer can move mountains, but one must have faith and not pray as Natasha and I used to as children, that the snow might turn into sugar—and then run out into the yard to see whether it had. No, but I am not praying for trifles now," he thought as he put his pipe down in a corner, and folding his hands, placed himself before the icon. Softened by memories of Princess Mary, he began to pray as he had not done for a long time. Tears were in his eyes and in his throat when the door opened and Lavrushka came in with some papers.

270.16.oldText: "Blockhead! Why do you come in without being called?" cried Nicholas, quickly changing his posture.

270.17.oldText: "From the governor," said Lavrushka in a sleepy voice. "A courier has arrived and there's a letter for you."

270.19.oldText: Nicholas took the two letters, one from his mother and the other from Sonya. He recognized them by the handwriting and opened Sonya's first. He had read only a few lines when he turned pale and his eyes opened wide with fear and joy.

270.21.oldText: Unable to sit still, he paced up and down the room holding the letter and reading it. He glanced through it, then read it again, and then once more, and standing still in the middle of the room raised his shoulders, stretching out his hands, with his mouth wide open and his eyes fixed. What he had just been praying for with confidence that God would hear him had come to pass; but Nicholas was as astonished as if it were something extraordinary and unexpected, and as if the very fact that it had happened so quickly proved it had come not from God—to whom he had prayed—but by some ordinary coincidence.

270.22.oldText: This unexpected and, as it seemed to Nicholas, completely voluntary letter from Sonya freed him from the knot that had bound him and from which there had seemed no escape. She wrote that the recent unfortunate events—the loss of nearly all the Rostovs' Moscow property—and the countess's repeatedly expressed wish that Nicholas should marry Princess Bolkonskaya, together with his silence and coldness of late, had all combined to make her decide to release him from his promise and set him completely free.

270.23.oldText: It would be too painful to me to think that I might be a cause of sorrow or conflict in the family that has been so good to me (she wrote), and my love has no aim but the happiness of those I love; so, Nicholas, I beg you to consider yourself free, and to be assured that, in spite of everything, no one can love you more than does

270.25.oldText: Both letters were written from Troitsa. The other, from the countess, described their last days in Moscow, their departure, the fire, and the destruction of all their property. In this letter the countess also mentioned that Prince Andrew was among the wounded traveling with them; his condition was very critical, but the doctor said there was now more hope. Sonya and Natasha were nursing him.

270.26.oldText: Next day Nicholas took his mother's letter and went to see Princess Mary. Neither he nor she said a word about what "Natasha nursing him" might mean, but thanks to this letter Nicholas suddenly became almost as intimate with the princess as if they were relatives.

270.27.oldText: The following day he saw Princess Mary off on her journey to Yaroslavl, and a few days later left to rejoin his regiment.

271.0.oldText: Sonya's letter from Troitsa, which had come as an answer to Nicholas's prayer, was prompted by this: the thought of getting Nicholas married to an heiress occupied the old countess's mind more and more. She knew that Sonya was the chief obstacle to this, and Sonya's life in the countess's house had grown harder and harder, especially after they received a letter from Nicholas telling of his meeting with Princess Mary in Bogucharovo. The countess let no opportunity slip for making humiliating or cruel remarks to Sonya.

271.1.oldText: But a few days before they left Moscow, moved and excited by all that was going on, the countess called Sonya to her and, instead of reproaching and making demands, tearfully begged her to sacrifice herself and repay all that the family had done for her by breaking off her engagement with Nicholas.

271.2.oldText: "I shall not be at peace till you promise me this."

271.3.oldText: Sonya burst into hysterical tears and replied through her sobs that she would do anything and was prepared for anything, but gave no actual promise and could not bring herself to do what was demanded of her. She had to sacrifice herself for the family that had raised her. Sacrificing herself for others was Sonya's habit. Her position in the house was such that only through sacrifice could she prove her worth, and she was accustomed to this and loved doing it. But in all her previous acts of self-sacrifice she had been happily aware that they raised her in her own esteem and in that of others, making her more worthy of Nicholas, whom she loved more than anything in the world. But now they wanted her to sacrifice the very thing that was the entire reward for her self-sacrifice and the whole meaning of her life. And for the first time she felt bitterness against those who had been her benefactors only to torment her more; she felt jealous of Natasha, who had never experienced anything of the sort, had never needed to sacrifice herself, but made others sacrifice themselves for her, and yet was loved by everybody. And for the first time Sonya felt that out of her pure, quiet love for Nicholas, a passionate feeling was beginning to grow—stronger than principle, virtue, or religion. Under the influence of this feeling, Sonya—whose life of dependence had taught her to be secretive—having answered the countess in vague general terms, avoided further discussion and resolved to wait until she saw Nicholas, not to set him free but on the contrary, at that meeting, to bind him to her forever.

271.4.oldText: The bustle and terror of the Rostovs' last days in Moscow stifled the gloomy thoughts that oppressed Sonya. She was glad to find escape in practical activity. But when she heard of Prince Andrew's presence in their house, despite her sincere pity for him and for Natasha, she was seized by a joyful and superstitious feeling that God did not intend her to be separated from Nicholas. She knew that Natasha loved no one but Prince Andrew and had never stopped loving him. She knew that being thrown together again under such terrible circumstances, they would fall in love once more, and that Nicholas would then be unable to marry Princess Mary, as they would be too closely connected by family ties. Despite all the terror of what had happened during those last days and during the first days of their journey, this feeling that Providence was intervening in her personal affairs cheered Sonya.

271.5.oldText: At the Troitsa monastery the Rostovs first broke their journey for a whole day.

271.6.oldText: Three large rooms were assigned to them in the monastery hostelry, one of which was occupied by Prince Andrew. The wounded man was much better that day, and Natasha was sitting with him. In the next room sat the count and countess, respectfully conversing with the prior, who was visiting them as old acquaintances and benefactors of the monastery. Sonya was there too, tormented by curiosity about what Prince Andrew and Natasha were talking about. She heard the sound of their voices through the door. That door opened and Natasha came out, looking excited. Not noticing the monk who had risen to greet her and was drawing back the wide sleeve on his right arm, she went straight to Sonya and took her hand.

271.8.oldText: Natasha went up to the monk for his blessing, and he advised her to pray for the help of God and His saint.

271.9.oldText: As soon as the prior withdrew, Natasha took her friend by the hand and went with her into the unoccupied room.

271.10.oldText: "Sonya, will he live?" she asked. "Sonya, how happy I am, and how unhappy!... Sonya, dear, everything is as it used to be. If only he lives! He cannot... because... because... of..." and Natasha burst into tears.

271.12.oldText: Sonya was no less agitated than her friend—by Natasha's fear and grief and by her own personal feelings, which she shared with no one. Sobbing, she kissed and comforted Natasha. "If only he lives!" she thought. Having wept, talked, and wiped away their tears, the two friends went together to Prince Andrew's door. Natasha opened it cautiously and glanced into the room, Sonya standing beside her at the half-open door.

271.13.oldText: Prince Andrew was lying propped high on three pillows. His pale face was calm, his eyes closed, and they could see his steady breathing.

271.16.oldText: "It's that, that..." said Sonya, with a white face and trembling lips.

271.17.oldText: Natasha softly closed the door and went with Sonya to the window, not yet understanding what she was telling her.

271.18.oldText: "You remember," said Sonya with a solemn and frightened expression, "you remember when I looked in the mirror for you... at Otradnoe at Christmas? Do you remember what I saw?"

271.19.oldText: "Yes, yes!" cried Natasha, opening her eyes wide and vaguely recalling that Sonya had told her something about Prince Andrew whom she had seen lying down.

271.20.oldText: "You remember?" Sonya went on. "I saw it then and told everybody, you and Dunyasha. I saw him lying on a bed," said she, making a gesture with her hand and a lifted finger at each detail, "and that he had his eyes closed and was covered just with a pink quilt, and that his hands were folded," she concluded, convincing herself that the details she had just seen were exactly what she had seen in the mirror.

271.21.oldText: In fact she had seen nothing then but had mentioned the first thing that came into her head, but what she had invented then now seemed to her as real as any other memory. She not only remembered what she had then said—that he turned to look at her and smiled and was covered with something red—but was firmly convinced that she had seen and said that he was covered with a pink quilt and that his eyes were closed.

271.24.oldText: "Oh, I don't know, it's all so strange," replied Sonya, clutching at her head.

271.25.oldText: A few minutes later Prince Andrew rang and Natasha went to him, but Sonya, feeling unusually excited and touched, remained at the window thinking about the strangeness of what had occurred.

271.26.oldText: They had an opportunity that day to send letters to the army, and the countess was writing to her son.

271.27.oldText: "Sonya!" said the countess, raising her eyes from her letter as her niece passed. "Sonya, won't you write to Nicholas?" She spoke in a soft, tremulous voice, and in the weary eyes that looked over her spectacles Sonya read all that the countess meant to convey with these words. Those eyes expressed pleading, shame at having to ask, fear of a refusal, and readiness for merciless hatred in case of such refusal.

271.28.oldText: Sonya went up to the countess and, kneeling down, kissed her hand.

271.29.oldText: "Yes, Mama, I will write," said she.

271.30.oldText: Sonya was softened, excited, and touched by all that had happened that day, especially by the mysterious fulfillment she had just seen of her vision. Now that she knew the renewal of Natasha's relationship with Prince Andrew would prevent Nicholas from marrying Princess Mary, she felt a joyful return of that self-sacrificing spirit she was accustomed to and loved to live by. So with a joyful consciousness of performing a noble deed—interrupted several times by tears that blurred her velvety black eyes—she wrote that touching letter the arrival of which had so amazed Nicholas.

272.0.oldText: The officer and soldiers who had arrested Pierre treated him with hostility but also with respect in the guardhouse to which he was taken. In their attitude toward him could still be felt both uncertainty as to who he might be—perhaps a very important person—and hostility resulting from their recent personal conflict with him.

272.1.oldText: But when the guard was relieved next morning, Pierre felt that for the new guard—both officers and men—he was not as interesting as he had been to his captors; and in fact, the second day's guard did not recognize in this big, stout man in a peasant coat the vigorous person who had fought so desperately with the marauder and the escort and had uttered those solemn words about saving a child. They saw in him only Prisoner No. 17 of the captured Russians, arrested and held for some reason by order of the Higher Command. If they noticed anything remarkable about Pierre, it was only his untroubled, meditative concentration and thoughtfulness, and the way he spoke French, which struck them as surprisingly good. Despite this, he was placed that day with the other arrested suspects, as the separate room he had occupied was needed by an officer.

272.2.oldText: All the Russians confined with Pierre were men of the lowest class, and recognizing him as a gentleman, they all avoided him—especially as he spoke French. Pierre felt sad hearing them make fun of him.

272.3.oldText: That evening he learned that all these prisoners (he probably among them) were to be tried for arson. On the third day he was taken with the others to a house where a French general with a white mustache sat with two colonels and other Frenchmen with scarves on their arms. With the precision and formality customary in addressing prisoners—intended to preclude human frailty—Pierre, like the others, was questioned as to who he was, where he had been, with what purpose, and so on.

272.4.oldText: These questions, like questions at trials in general, left the essence of the matter aside, shut out the possibility of that essence being revealed, and were designed only to form a channel through which the judges wished the answers to flow so as to lead to the desired result—namely, a conviction. As soon as Pierre began to say anything that didn't fit that aim, the channel was removed and the water flowed to waste. Pierre felt, moreover, what the accused always feel at their trial—perplexity as to why these questions were put to him. He had a feeling that it was only out of condescension or a kind of courtesy that this device of placing a channel was employed. He knew he was in these men's power, that only by force had they brought him there, that force alone gave them the right to demand answers to their questions, and that the sole purpose of this assembly was to convict him. And so, since they had the power and wish to convict him, this procedure of inquiry and trial seemed unnecessary. It was obvious that any answer would lead to conviction. When asked what he was doing when arrested, Pierre replied in a rather dramatic manner that he was returning a child he had saved from the flames to its parents. Why had he fought the marauder? Pierre answered that he "was protecting a woman" and that "to protect a woman being attacked was the duty of every man; that..." They interrupted him, for this was not to the point. Why was he in the yard of a burning house, where witnesses had seen him? He replied that he had gone out to see what was happening in Moscow. Again they interrupted him: they had not asked where he was going, but why he was found near the fire. Who was he? they asked, repeating their first question, which he had declined to answer. Again he said he could not answer it.

272.5.oldText: "Put that down. That's bad... very bad," sternly remarked the general with the white mustache and red, flushed face.

272.6.oldText: On the fourth day, fires broke out on the Zubovsky rampart.

272.7.oldText: Pierre and thirteen others were moved to the coach house of a merchant's house near the Crimean bridge. On his way through the streets, Pierre was choked by the smoke that seemed to hang over the whole city. Fires were visible on all sides. He did not then realize the significance of the burning of Moscow, and looked at the fires with horror.

272.8.oldText: He spent four days in the coach house near the Crimean bridge and during that time learned from the talk of the French soldiers that all those confined there were awaiting a decision from the marshal—any day now. Which marshal, Pierre could not find out from the soldiers. Evidently for them "the marshal" represented a very high and rather mysterious power.

272.9.oldText: These first days, before the eighth of September when the prisoners were brought up for a second examination, were the hardest of all for Pierre.

273.0.oldText: On the eighth of September an officer—a very important one, judging by the respect the guards showed him—entered the coach house where the prisoners were. This officer, probably someone on the staff, held a paper in his hand and called over all the Russians there, naming Pierre as "the man who does not give his name." Glancing casually and indifferently at all the prisoners, he ordered the officer in charge to have them decently dressed and tidied up before taking them to the marshal. An hour later a squad of soldiers arrived and Pierre with thirteen others was led to the Virgin's Field. It was a fine day, sunny after rain, and the air was unusually pure. The smoke did not hang low as on the day Pierre had been taken from the guardhouse on the Zubovsky rampart, but rose through the clear air in columns. No flames were seen, but columns of smoke rose on all sides, and all Moscow, as far as Pierre could see, was one vast charred ruin. On all sides there were waste spaces with only stoves and chimney stacks still standing, and here and there the blackened walls of some brick houses. Pierre gazed at the ruins and did not recognize districts he had known well. Here and there he could see churches that had not burned. The Kremlin, undestroyed, gleamed white in the distance with its towers and the belfry of Ivan the Great. The domes of the New Convent of the Virgin glittered brightly, and its bells were ringing particularly clearly. These bells reminded Pierre that it was Sunday and the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin. But there seemed to be no one to celebrate this holiday: everywhere were blackened ruins, and the few Russians to be seen were tattered, frightened people who tried to hide when they saw the French.

273.1.oldText: It was plain that the Russian nest was ruined and destroyed, but in place of the Russian order of life that had been destroyed, Pierre unconsciously sensed that a quite different, firm, French order had been established over this ruined nest. He felt this in the looks of the soldiers who, marching in regular ranks briskly and cheerfully, were escorting him and the other prisoners; he felt it in the looks of an important French official in a carriage and pair driven by a soldier, whom they met on the way. He felt it in the merry sounds of regimental music from the left side of the field, and felt and realized it especially from the list of prisoners the French officer had read out that morning. Pierre had been taken by one set of soldiers and led first to one and then to another place with dozens of other men, and it seemed that they might have forgotten him or mixed him up with the others. But no: the answers he had given when questioned had come back to him in his designation as "the man who does not give his name," and under that label, which seemed to Pierre terrible, they were now leading him somewhere with unhesitating confidence on their faces—assurance that he and all the other prisoners were exactly the ones they wanted and that they were being taken to the proper place. Pierre felt himself to be an insignificant chip fallen among the wheels of a machine whose workings he did not understand but which was operating smoothly.

273.2.oldText: He and the other prisoners were taken to the right side of the Virgin's Field, to a large white house with an immense garden not far from the convent. This was Prince Shcherbatov's house, where Pierre had often been in better days, and which, as he learned from the talk of the soldiers, was now occupied by the marshal, the Duke of Eckmuhl (Davout).

273.3.oldText: They were taken to the entrance and led into the house one by one. Pierre was the sixth to enter. He was conducted through a glass gallery, an anteroom, and a hall—all familiar to him—into a long low study at whose door stood an adjutant.

273.4.oldText: Davout, with spectacles perched on his nose, sat bent over a table at the far end of the room. Pierre went close up to him, but Davout, evidently consulting a paper before him, did not look up. Without raising his eyes, he said in a low voice:

273.6.oldText: Pierre was silent because he was incapable of uttering a word. To him Davout was not merely a French general, but a man notorious for his cruelty. Looking at that cold face as Davout sat like a stern schoolmaster willing to wait for an answer, Pierre felt that every instant of delay might cost him his life; but he did not know what to say. He did not dare to repeat what he had said at his first examination, yet to reveal his rank and position was dangerous and embarrassing. So he was silent. But before he had decided what to do, Davout raised his head, pushed his spectacles back on his forehead, narrowed his eyes, and looked intently at him.

273.7.oldText: "I know that man," he said in a cold, measured tone, evidently calculated to frighten Pierre.

273.8.oldText: The chill that had been running down Pierre's back now seized his head like a vise.

273.9.oldText: "You cannot know me, General. I have never seen you..."

273.10.oldText: "He is a Russian spy," Davout interrupted, addressing another general who was present but whom Pierre had not noticed.

273.11.oldText: Davout turned away. With an unexpected resonance in his voice, Pierre began rapidly:

273.12.oldText: "No, monseigneur," he said, suddenly remembering that Davout was a duke. "No, monseigneur, you cannot have known me. I am a militia officer and have not left Moscow."

273.16.oldText: "Monseigneur!" exclaimed Pierre, not in an offended but in a pleading voice.

273.17.oldText: Davout looked up and gazed intently at him. For some seconds they looked at one another, and that look saved Pierre. Apart from conditions of war and law, that look established human relations between the two men. In that moment an immense number of things passed dimly through both their minds, and they realized that they were both children of humanity and were brothers.

273.18.oldText: At first glance, when Davout had only raised his head from the papers where human lives were indicated by numbers, Pierre was merely a case, and Davout could have shot him without burdening his conscience. But now he saw in him a human being. He reflected for a moment.

273.19.oldText: "How can you prove to me that you are telling the truth?" said Davout coldly.

273.20.oldText: Pierre remembered Ramballe, and named him and his regiment and the street where the house was.

273.21.oldText: "You are not what you say," returned Davout.

273.22.oldText: In a trembling, faltering voice Pierre began giving proofs of the truth of his statements.

273.23.oldText: But at that moment an adjutant entered and reported something to Davout.

273.24.oldText: Davout brightened at the adjutant's news and began buttoning up his uniform. He seemed to have completely forgotten Pierre.

273.25.oldText: When the adjutant reminded him of the prisoner, he jerked his head in Pierre's direction with a frown and ordered him to be led away. But where they were to take him Pierre did not know: back to the coach house, or to the place of execution his companions had pointed out as they crossed the Virgin's Field.

273.26.oldText: He turned his head and saw that the adjutant was putting another question to Davout.

273.27.oldText: "Yes, of course!" replied Davout, but what this "yes" meant, Pierre did not know.

273.28.oldText: Pierre could not afterward remember how he went, whether it was far, or in what direction. His faculties were completely numb; he was stupefied, and noticing nothing around him, he went on moving his legs as the others did till they all stopped and he stopped too. The only thought in his mind was: who had really sentenced him to death? Not the men on the commission that had first examined him—not one of them wished to or, evidently, could have done it. It was not Davout, who had looked at him in such a human way. In another moment Davout would have realized that he was doing wrong, but just then the adjutant had come in and interrupted him. The adjutant, too, had evidently had no evil intent, though he might have refrained from coming in. Then who was executing him, killing him, depriving him of life—him, Pierre, with all his memories, aspirations, hopes, and thoughts? Who was doing this? And Pierre felt that it was no one.

273.29.oldText: It was a system—a convergence of circumstances.

273.30.oldText: A system of some sort was killing him—Pierre—depriving him of life, of everything, annihilating him.

274.0.oldText: From Prince Shcherbatov's house the prisoners were led straight down the Virgin's Field, to the left of the nunnery, as far as a kitchen garden where a post had been set up. Beyond that post a fresh pit had been dug in the ground, and near the post and the pit a large crowd stood in a semicircle. The crowd consisted of a few Russians and many of Napoleon's soldiers who were not on duty—Germans, Italians, and Frenchmen, in a variety of uniforms. To the right and left of the post stood rows of French troops in blue uniforms with red epaulets, high boots, and shakos.

274.1.oldText: The prisoners were placed in a certain order, according to the list (Pierre was sixth), and were led to the post. Several drums suddenly began to beat on both sides of them, and at that sound Pierre felt as if part of his soul had been torn away. He lost the power of thinking or understanding. He could only hear and see. And he had only one wish—that the terrible thing that had to happen should happen quickly. Pierre looked round at his fellow prisoners and studied them.

274.2.oldText: The first two were convicts with shaven heads. One was tall and thin, the other dark, shaggy, and sinewy, with a flat nose. The third was a domestic servant, about forty-five years old, with graying hair and a plump, well-nourished body. The fourth was a peasant, a very handsome man with a broad, light-brown beard and black eyes. The fifth was a factory worker, a thin, sallow-faced boy of about eighteen in a loose coat.

274.3.oldText: Pierre heard the French consulting whether to shoot them one at a time or in pairs. "In pairs," replied the officer in command in a calm voice. There was a stir in the ranks of the soldiers, and it was obvious they were all hurrying—not as men hurry to do something they understand, but as people rush to finish a necessary but unpleasant and incomprehensible task.

274.4.oldText: A French official wearing a sash came up to the right of the row of prisoners and read out the sentence in Russian and in French.

274.5.oldText: Then two pairs of Frenchmen approached the condemned men and, at the officer's command, took the two convicts who stood first in the row. The convicts stopped when they reached the post, and while sacks were being brought, looked dumbly around as a wounded beast looks at an approaching hunter. One crossed himself continuously, the other scratched his back and made a movement of the lips resembling a smile. With hurried hands the soldiers blindfolded them, drawing the sacks over their heads, and tied them to the post.

274.6.oldText: Twelve sharpshooters with muskets stepped out of the ranks with a firm, regular tread and halted eight paces from the post. Pierre turned away to avoid seeing what was going to happen. Suddenly a crackling, rolling noise was heard, which seemed to him louder than the most terrific thunder, and he looked around. There was some smoke, and the Frenchmen were doing something near the pit, with pale faces and trembling hands. Two more prisoners were led up. In the same way and with similar looks, these two glanced vainly at the onlookers with only a silent appeal for protection in their eyes, evidently unable to understand or believe what was going to happen to them. They could not believe it because they alone knew what their lives meant to them, and so they neither understood nor believed that those lives could be taken from them.

274.7.oldText: Again Pierre did not wish to look and again turned away; but again the sound of a frightful explosion struck his ear, and at the same moment he saw smoke, blood, and the pale, scared faces of the Frenchmen who were again doing something by the post, their trembling hands getting in one another's way. Pierre, breathing heavily, looked around as if asking what it meant. The same question was expressed in all the faces that met his.

274.8.oldText: On the faces of all the Russians and of the French soldiers and officers without exception, he read the same dismay, horror, and inner conflict that were in his own heart. "But who, after all, is doing this? They are all suffering as I am. Who then is it? Who?" flashed for an instant through his mind.

274.9.oldText: "Sharpshooters of the 86th, forward!" shouted someone. The fifth prisoner, the one next to Pierre, was led away—alone. Pierre did not understand that he was saved, that he and the rest had been brought there only to witness the execution. With ever-growing horror, and no sense of joy or relief, he watched what was happening. The fifth man was the factory boy in the loose coat. The moment they laid hands on him he sprang aside in terror and clutched at Pierre. (Pierre shuddered and shook himself free.) The boy could not walk. They dragged him along, holding him up under the arms, and he screamed. When they got him to the post he grew quiet, as if he suddenly understood something. Whether he understood that screaming was useless, or whether he thought it impossible that men should kill him, he took his stand at the post, waiting to be blindfolded like the others, and like a wounded animal looked around him with glittering eyes.

274.10.oldText: Pierre was no longer able to turn away and close his eyes. His curiosity and agitation, like that of the whole crowd, reached the highest pitch at this fifth murder. Like the others, this fifth man seemed calm; he wrapped his loose coat closer and rubbed one bare foot with the other.

274.11.oldText: When they began to blindfold him, he himself adjusted the knot which hurt the back of his head; then when they propped him against the bloodstained post, he leaned back and, not being comfortable in that position, straightened himself, adjusted his feet, and leaned back again more comfortably. Pierre did not take his eyes from him and did not miss his slightest movement.

274.12.oldText: Probably a word of command was given, followed by the reports of eight muskets; but try as he would, Pierre could not afterwards remember hearing the slightest sound of the shots. He only saw how the worker suddenly sank down on the ropes that held him, how blood appeared in two places, how the ropes slackened under the weight of the hanging body, and how the worker sat down, his head hanging unnaturally and one leg bent under him. Pierre ran up to the post. No one stopped him. Pale, frightened people were doing something around the worker. The lower jaw of an old Frenchman with a thick mustache trembled as he untied the ropes. The body collapsed. The soldiers dragged it awkwardly from the post and began pushing it into the pit.

274.13.oldText: They all plainly and unmistakably knew that they were criminals who must hide the traces of their guilt as quickly as possible.

274.14.oldText: Pierre glanced into the pit and saw that the factory boy was lying with his knees close up to his head and one shoulder higher than the other. That shoulder rose and fell rhythmically and convulsively, but spadefuls of earth were already being thrown over the whole body. One of the soldiers, evidently suffering, shouted gruffly and angrily at Pierre to go back. But Pierre did not understand him and remained near the post, and no one drove him away.

274.15.oldText: When the pit had been filled up, a command was given. Pierre was taken back to his place, and the rows of troops on both sides of the post made a half turn and marched past it at a measured pace. The twenty-four sharpshooters with discharged muskets, standing in the center of the circle, ran back to their places as the companies passed by.

274.16.oldText: Pierre gazed now with dazed eyes at these sharpshooters who ran in pairs out of the circle. All but one rejoined their companies. This one, a young soldier, his face deathly pale, his cap pushed back, and his musket resting on the ground, still stood near the pit at the spot from which he had fired. He swayed like a drunken man, taking some steps forward and back to keep himself from falling. An old noncommissioned officer ran out of the ranks and, taking him by the elbow, dragged him to his company. The crowd of Russians and Frenchmen began to disperse. They all went away silently and with drooping heads.

274.17.oldText: "That will teach them to start fires," said one of the Frenchmen.

274.18.oldText: Pierre glanced at the speaker and saw that it was a soldier who was trying to find some comfort after what had been done, but could not. Without finishing what he had begun to say, he made a hopeless gesture with his arm and went away.

276.0.oldText: Twenty-three soldiers, three officers, and two officials were confined in the shed where Pierre had been placed and where he remained for four weeks.

276.1.oldText: When Pierre remembered them afterward, they all seemed misty figures to him except Platon Karataev, who always remained in his mind the most vivid and precious memory and the embodiment of everything Russian, kindly, and round. When Pierre saw his neighbor the next morning at dawn, the first impression of him—as of something round—was fully confirmed: Platon's whole figure—in a French overcoat belted with a cord, a soldier's cap, and bast shoes—was round. His head was perfectly round, his back, chest, shoulders, and even his arms, which he held as if ever ready to embrace something, were rounded; his pleasant smile and his large, gentle brown eyes were round too.

276.2.oldText: Platon Karataev must have been about fifty, judging by his stories of campaigns he had been in, told like an old soldier. He did not know his own age and was quite unable to determine it. But his brilliantly white, strong teeth—which showed in two unbroken semicircles when he laughed, as he often did—were all sound and good. There was not a gray hair in his beard or on his head, and his whole body gave an impression of suppleness and especially of firmness and endurance.

276.3.oldText: His face, despite its fine, rounded wrinkles, had an expression of innocence and youth; his voice was pleasant and musical. But the chief peculiarity of his speech was its directness and aptness. It was evident that he never considered what he had said or was going to say, and consequently the speed and rightness of his delivery had an irresistible persuasiveness.

276.4.oldText: His physical strength and agility during the first days of his imprisonment were such that he seemed not to know what fatigue and sickness meant. Every night before lying down he said: "Lord, lay me down as a stone and raise me up as a loaf!" And every morning on getting up he said: "I lay down and curled up, I get up and shake myself." And indeed he only had to lie down to fall asleep like a stone, and he only had to shake himself to be ready without a moment's delay for any work, just as children are ready to play the instant they wake. He could do everything—not very well but not badly. He baked, cooked, sewed, planed, and mended boots. He was always busy, and only at night allowed himself conversation—which he loved—and songs. He did not sing like a trained singer who knows he is being listened to, but like the birds, evidently giving vent to the sounds in the same way that one stretches or walks about to relieve stiffness. The sounds were always high-pitched, mournful, delicate, and almost feminine, and his face at such times was very serious.

276.5.oldText: Having been taken prisoner and allowed his beard to grow, he seemed to have thrown off everything that had been forced upon him—everything military and foreign to his nature—and had returned to his former peasant ways.

276.6.oldText: "A soldier on leave—a shirt worn outside the trousers," he would say.

276.7.oldText: He did not like talking about his life as a soldier, though he did not complain, and often mentioned that he had never once been flogged during his whole army service. When he told stories it was generally from old and evidently treasured memories of his "Christian" life, as he called his peasant existence. The proverbs that filled his speech were not the coarse and crude ones soldiers use, but those folk sayings which, taken out of context, seem so insignificant, but which used at the right moment suddenly acquire a significance of profound wisdom.

276.8.oldText: He would often say the exact opposite of what he had said on a previous occasion, yet both would be right. He liked to talk and he talked well, adorning his speech with terms of endearment and folk sayings which Pierre thought he invented himself. But the chief charm of his talk lay in the fact that the most common events—sometimes just such as Pierre had witnessed without taking notice of them—assumed in Karataev's telling a character of solemn meaning. He liked to hear the folk tales one of the soldiers told in the evenings (they were always the same), but most of all he liked to hear stories of real life. He would smile joyfully while listening to such stories, now and then putting in a word or asking a question to make the moral beauty of what he was told clear to himself. Karataev had no attachments, friendships, or love as Pierre understood them, but loved and lived warmly with everything life brought him into contact with, particularly with people—not any particular person, but those with whom he happened to be. He loved his dog, his comrades, the French, and Pierre who was his neighbor; but Pierre felt that despite Karataev's affectionate tenderness for him (by which he unconsciously gave Pierre's spiritual life its due), he would not have grieved for a moment at parting from him. And Pierre began to feel the same way toward Karataev.

276.9.oldText: To all the other prisoners, Platon Karataev seemed a most ordinary soldier. They called him "little falcon" or "Platosha," teased him good-naturedly, and sent him on errands. But to Pierre he always remained what he had seemed that first night: an unfathomable, rounded, eternal personification of the spirit of simplicity and truth.

276.10.oldText: Platon Karataev knew nothing by heart except his prayers. When he began to speak he seemed not to know how he would finish.

276.11.oldText: Sometimes Pierre, struck by the meaning of his words, would ask him to repeat them, but Platon could never recall what he had said a moment before, just as he could never repeat to Pierre the words of his favorite song: native and birch tree and my heart is sick came up in it, but when spoken rather than sung, no meaning could be extracted. He did not, and could not, understand the meaning of words apart from their context. Every word and action of his was the expression of an activity unknown to him, which was his life. But his life, as he saw it, had no meaning as a separate thing. It had meaning only as part of a whole of which he was always conscious. His words and actions flowed from him as evenly, inevitably, and spontaneously as fragrance from a flower. He could not understand the value or significance of any word or deed taken separately.

277.0.oldText: When Princess Mary heard from Nicholas that her brother was with the Rostovs at Yaroslavl, she at once prepared to go there, despite her aunt's efforts to dissuade her—and not merely to go herself but to take her nephew with her. Whether it was difficult or easy, possible or impossible, she did not ask and did not want to know: it was her duty, not only to herself, to be near her brother who was perhaps dying, but to do everything possible to bring his son to him, and so she prepared to set off. That she had not heard from Prince Andrew himself, Princess Mary attributed to his being too weak to write, or to his considering the long journey too hard and too dangerous for her and his son.

277.1.oldText: In a few days Princess Mary was ready to start. Her vehicles were the huge family coach in which she had traveled to Voronezh, a half-open carriage, and a baggage cart. With her traveled Mademoiselle Bourienne, little Nicholas and his tutor, her old nurse, three maids, Tikhon, and a young footman and courier her aunt had sent to accompany her.

277.2.oldText: The usual route through Moscow was out of the question, and the roundabout way Princess Mary was obliged to take through Lipetsk, Ryazan, Vladimir, and Shuya was very long and, since post horses were not available everywhere, very difficult, and near Ryazan—where the French were said to have appeared—even dangerous.

277.3.oldText: During this difficult journey, Mademoiselle Bourienne, Dessalles, and Princess Mary's servants were astonished at her energy and strength of spirit. She went to bed later and rose earlier than any of them, and no difficulties daunted her. Thanks to her activity and energy, which inspired her fellow travelers, they approached Yaroslavl by the end of the second week.

277.4.oldText: The last days of her stay in Voronezh had been the happiest of her life. Her love for Rostov no longer tormented or agitated her. It filled her whole soul, had become an integral part of herself, and she no longer fought against it. She had become convinced that she loved and was loved, though she never said this to herself in words. She had become convinced of it at her last meeting with Nicholas, when he had come to tell her that her brother was with the Rostovs. Not by a single word had Nicholas alluded to the fact that Prince Andrew's relationship with Natasha might, if he recovered, be renewed; but Princess Mary saw from his face that he knew and thought of this.

277.5.oldText: Yet despite that, his attitude toward her—considerate, delicate, and loving—not only remained unchanged, but it sometimes seemed to Princess Mary that he was even glad that the family connection between them allowed him to express his friendship more freely. She knew that she loved for the first and only time in her life, and felt that she was loved, and was happy in that knowledge.

277.6.oldText: But this happiness on one side of her spiritual nature did not prevent her from feeling grief for her brother with full force; on the contrary, that spiritual peace on one side made it all the more possible for her to give full expression to her feeling for her brother. That feeling was so strong at the moment of leaving Voronezh that those who saw her off, looking at her careworn, despairing face, felt certain she would fall ill on the journey. But the very difficulties and demands of the journey, which she took so actively in hand, saved her for a while from her grief and gave her strength.

277.7.oldText: As always happens when traveling, Princess Mary thought only of the journey itself, forgetting its purpose. But as she approached Yaroslavl, the thought of what might await her there—not after many days but that very evening—again presented itself, and her agitation reached its peak.

277.8.oldText: The courier who had been sent ahead to find out where the Rostovs were staying in Yaroslavl and in what condition Prince Andrew was, met the big coach just entering the town gates and was appalled by the terrible pallor of the princess's face looking out at him from the window.

277.9.oldText: "I have found out everything, your excellency: the Rostovs are staying at the merchant Bronnikov's house, in the square not far from here, right above the Volga," said the courier.

277.10.oldText: Princess Mary looked at him with frightened inquiry, not understanding why he did not reply to what she most wanted to know: how was her brother? Mademoiselle Bourienne asked that question for her.

277.12.oldText: "His excellency is staying in the same house with them."

277.13.oldText: "Then he is alive," thought Princess Mary, and asked in a low voice: "How is he?"

277.15.oldText: What "still the same" might mean, Princess Mary did not ask, but with an unnoticed glance at little seven-year-old Nicholas—who was sitting in front of her looking with pleasure at the town—she bowed her head and did not raise it again until the heavy coach, rumbling, shaking, and swaying, came to a stop. The carriage steps clattered as they were let down.

277.16.oldText: The carriage door opened. On the left there was water—a great river—and on the right a porch. There were people at the entrance: servants, and a rosy girl with a large plait of black hair, smiling in a way that seemed to Princess Mary unpleasantly artificial. (This was Sonya.) Princess Mary ran up the steps. "This way, this way!" said the girl with the same artificial smile, and the princess found herself in the hall facing an elderly woman of Eastern appearance, who came quickly toward her with a look of emotion. This was the countess. She embraced Princess Mary and kissed her.

277.17.oldText: "My child!" she murmured, "I love you and have known you a long time."

277.19.oldText: Despite her emotion, Princess Mary realized that this was the countess and that she must say something to her. Hardly knowing how she managed it, she spoke a few polite phrases in French in the same tone as those addressed to her, and asked: "How is he?"

277.20.oldText: "The doctor says he is not in danger," said the countess, but as she spoke she raised her eyes with a sigh, and her gesture conveyed a contradiction of her words.

277.21.oldText: "Where is he? Can I see him—can I?" asked the princess.

277.22.oldText: "One moment, Princess, one moment, my dear! Is this his son?" said the countess, turning to little Nicholas who was coming in with Dessalles. "There will be room for everybody; this is a big house. Oh, what a lovely boy!"

277.23.oldText: The countess took Princess Mary into the drawing room, where Sonya was talking to Mademoiselle Bourienne. The countess caressed the boy, and the old count came in and welcomed the princess. He had changed very much since she had last seen him. Then he had been a brisk, cheerful, self-assured old man; now he seemed a pitiful, bewildered person. While talking to Princess Mary he kept looking around as if asking everyone whether he was doing the right thing. After the destruction of Moscow and of his property, thrown out of his accustomed groove, he seemed to have lost his sense of his own importance and to feel that there was no longer a place for him in life.

277.24.oldText: Despite her one desire to see her brother as soon as possible, and her irritation that at the moment when all she wanted was to see him they were trying to entertain her and pretending to admire her nephew, the princess noticed all that was going on around her and felt the necessity of submitting for a time to this new order of things she had entered. She knew it was necessary, and though it was hard for her, she was not angry with these people.

277.26.oldText: Princess Mary turned to Sonya and, trying to suppress the hostile feeling that arose in her toward the girl, she kissed her. But she felt oppressed by the fact that the mood of everyone around her was so far from what was in her own heart.

277.28.oldText: "He is downstairs. Natasha is with him," answered Sonya, flushing. "We have sent to ask. I think you must be tired, Princess."

277.29.oldText: Tears of frustration showed in Princess Mary's eyes. She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to go to him, when light, eager, and seemingly buoyant steps were heard at the door. The princess looked around and saw Natasha coming in, almost running—that Natasha whom she had liked so little at their meeting in Moscow long before.

277.30.oldText: But hardly had the princess looked at Natasha's face before she realized that here was a true companion in her grief, and therefore a friend. She ran to meet her, embraced her, and began to cry on her shoulder.

277.32.oldText: There was only one expression on her agitated face when she ran into the drawing room—that of love: boundless love for him, for her, and for all that was close to the man she loved; and of pity, suffering for others, and a passionate desire to give herself entirely to helping them. It was plain that at that moment there was in Natasha's heart no thought of herself or of her own relationship with Prince Andrew.

277.33.oldText: Princess Mary, with her acute sensitivity, understood all this at the first glance at Natasha's face, and wept on her shoulder with sorrowful joy.

277.35.oldText: Princess Mary raised her head, dried her eyes, and turned to Natasha. She felt that from her she would be able to understand and learn everything.

277.37.oldText: She felt that it was impossible to ask, or to answer, in words. Natasha's face and eyes would have to tell her everything more clearly and deeply.

277.38.oldText: Natasha was gazing at her but seemed afraid and in doubt whether to say all she knew or not; she seemed to feel that before those luminous eyes that penetrated into the very depths of her heart, it was impossible not to tell the whole truth as she saw it. And suddenly Natasha's lips twitched, ugly wrinkles gathered round her mouth, and covering her face with her hands, she burst into sobs.

277.40.oldText: But she still hoped, and asked in words she herself did not trust:

277.43.oldText: They sat a little while downstairs near his room until they had stopped crying and were able to go to him with calm faces.

277.44.oldText: "How has his whole illness gone? Is it long since he grew worse? When did this happen?" Princess Mary asked.

277.45.oldText: Natasha told her that at first there had been danger from his feverish condition and the pain he suffered, but at Troitsa that had passed and the doctor had only been afraid of gangrene. That danger had also passed. When they reached Yaroslavl, the wound had begun to fester (Natasha knew all about such things as festering), and the doctor had said the festering might take a normal course. Then fever set in, but the doctor had said the fever was not very serious.

278.0.oldText: When Natasha opened Prince Andrew's door with a familiar movement and let Princess Mary pass into the room before her, the princess felt the sobs in her throat. Hard as she had tried to prepare herself and now tried to remain calm, she knew she would be unable to look at him without tears.

278.1.oldText: The princess understood what Natasha had meant by the words: "two days ago this suddenly happened." She understood those words to mean that he had suddenly softened, and that this softening and gentleness were signs of approaching death. As she stepped toward the door she already saw in her imagination Andrew's face as she remembered it in childhood—a gentle, mild, compassionate face which he had rarely shown, and which therefore affected her deeply. She was sure he would speak soft, tender words to her such as her father had said before his death, and that she would not be able to bear it and would burst into sobs in his presence. Yet sooner or later it had to be, and she went in. The sobs rose higher and higher in her throat as she more and more clearly made out his form, and her nearsighted eyes tried to distinguish his features—and then she saw his face and met his gaze.

278.2.oldText: He was lying in a squirrel-fur dressing gown on a divan, surrounded by pillows. He was thin and pale. In one thin, translucently white hand he held a handkerchief, while with the other he slowly stroked the delicate mustache he had grown, moving his fingers slowly. His eyes gazed at them as they entered.

278.3.oldText: On seeing his face and meeting his eyes, Princess Mary's pace suddenly slackened; she felt her tears dry up and her sobs cease. She suddenly felt guilty and grew timid, catching the expression of his face and eyes.

278.4.oldText: "But what am I guilty of?" she asked herself. And his cold, stern look replied: "Because you are alive and thinking of the living, while I..."

278.5.oldText: In the deep gaze that seemed to look not outward but inward, there was an almost hostile expression as he slowly regarded his sister and Natasha.

278.6.oldText: He kissed his sister, holding her hand in his as was their custom.

278.7.oldText: "How are you, Mary? How did you manage to get here?" said he in a voice as calm and detached as his look.

278.8.oldText: Had he screamed in agony, that scream would not have struck such horror into Princess Mary's heart as the tone of his voice.

278.9.oldText: "And have you brought little Nicholas?" he asked in the same slow, quiet manner, with an obvious effort to remember.

278.10.oldText: "How are you now?" said Princess Mary, herself surprised at what she was saying.

278.11.oldText: "That, my dear, you must ask the doctor," he replied, and again making an evident effort to be warm, he said with his lips only (his words clearly did not match his thoughts):

278.14.oldText: Princess Mary pressed his hand. The pressure made him wince just perceptibly. He was silent, and she did not know what to say. She now understood what had happened to him two days before. In his words, his tone, and especially in that calm, almost hostile look could be felt an estrangement from everything belonging to this world—terrible in one who is alive. Evidently only with an effort did he understand anything living; but it was clear that he failed to understand not because he lacked the ability, but because he understood something else—something the living did not and could not understand—and which wholly occupied his mind.

278.15.oldText: "There, you see how strangely fate has brought us together," said he, breaking the silence and pointing to Natasha. "She looks after me all the time."

278.16.oldText: Princess Mary heard him and did not understand how he could say such a thing. He, the sensitive, tender Prince Andrew—how could he say that, in front of the woman he loved and who loved him? Had he expected to live, he could not have spoken those words in that offensively cold tone. If he had not known he was dying, how could he have failed to pity her, and how could he speak like that in her presence? The only explanation was that he was indifferent, because something else, much more important, had been revealed to him.

278.17.oldText: The conversation was cold and disconnected and continually broke off.

278.19.oldText: Prince Andrew did not notice that she called his sister Mary; and only after calling her so in his presence did Natasha notice it herself.

278.21.oldText: "They told her that all Moscow has been burned down, and that..."

278.22.oldText: Natasha stopped. It was impossible to talk. It was plain that he was making an effort to listen but could not.

278.23.oldText: "Yes, they say it's burned," he said. "It's a great pity," and he gazed straight before him, absently stroking his mustache with his fingers.

278.24.oldText: "And so you have met Count Nicholas, Mary?" Prince Andrew suddenly said, evidently wishing to speak pleasantly to them. "He wrote here that he took a great liking to you," he went on simply and calmly, evidently unable to understand all the complex significance his words had for living people. "If you liked him too, it would be a good thing for you to get married," he added rather more quickly, as if pleased at finding words he had long been seeking.

278.25.oldText: Princess Mary heard his words but they had no meaning for her except as proof of how far away he now was from everything living.

278.26.oldText: "Why talk of me?" she said quietly and glanced at Natasha.

278.27.oldText: Natasha, who felt her glance, did not look at her. All three were again silent.

278.28.oldText: "Andrew, would you like..." Princess Mary suddenly said in a trembling voice, "would you like to see little Nicholas? He is always talking about you!"

278.29.oldText: Prince Andrew smiled just perceptibly and for the first time, but Princess Mary, who knew his face so well, saw with horror that he did not smile with pleasure or affection for his son, but with quiet, gentle irony—because he thought she was trying what she believed to be the last means of rousing him.

278.30.oldText: "Yes, I shall be very glad to see him. Is he quite well?"

278.32.oldText: When Nicholas had been led away, Princess Mary again went up to her brother, kissed him, and unable to hold back her tears any longer, began to cry.

278.35.oldText: Princess Mary nodded her head, weeping.

278.39.oldText: When Princess Mary began to cry, he understood that she was crying at the thought that little Nicholas would be left without a father. With a great effort he tried to return to life and to see things from their point of view.

278.41.oldText: "The birds of the air neither sow nor reap, yet your Father feeds them," he said to himself, and wished to say to Princess Mary; "but no, they will take it their own way. They won't understand! They can't understand that all those feelings they prize so—all our feelings, all those ideas that seem so important to us—are unnecessary. We cannot understand one another." And he remained silent.

278.42.oldText: Prince Andrew's little son was seven. He could scarcely read and knew nothing. After that day he lived through many things, gaining knowledge, observation, and experience; but had he possessed all the faculties he later acquired, he could not have had a better or more profound understanding of the meaning of the scene he had witnessed between his father, Mary, and Natasha than he had then. He understood it completely, and leaving the room without crying, went silently up to Natasha—who had come out with him—and looked shyly at her with his beautiful, thoughtful eyes. Then his upturned, rosy upper lip trembled, and leaning his head against her, he began to cry.

278.43.oldText: After that he avoided Dessalles and the countess who caressed him, and either sat alone or came timidly to Princess Mary or to Natasha, of whom he seemed even fonder than of his aunt, and clung to them quietly and shyly.

278.44.oldText: When Princess Mary had left Prince Andrew she fully understood what Natasha's face had told her. She did not speak any more to Natasha about hopes of saving his life. She took turns with her beside his sofa, and did not cry anymore, but prayed continually, turning in her soul to that Eternal and Unfathomable, whose presence above the dying man was now so clearly felt.

286.9.oldText: 'It's not too late yet, Your Highness—the enemy hasn't pulled back. If you would order an attack... Otherwise the Guards won't even get a glimpse of smoke.'

335.5.oldText: "What—Petersburg? What is Petersburg? Who's in Petersburg?" he asked, though only of himself. "Oh yes, a long time ago—before all this happened—I did mean to go to Petersburg for some reason," he reflected. "Why? But maybe I will go... What a good, considerate fellow he is!" he thought, looking at Savelich. "And what a nice smile!"

352.27.oldText: "Well, it won't be long now. Next summer I'll take him to Petersburg," said Nicholas. "Yes, Pierre always was a dreamer and always will be," he continued, returning to the argument that had clearly upset him. "Well, what business is it of mine what goes on there—Arakcheyev's misconduct, and all the rest? What business was it of mine when we got married and I had so many debts that they were threatening to put me in prison? And what about your mother? She could never understand. And now—in a year or two I could show them Otradnoe! And if everything continues as it is, in another three years I'll have paid off all the debts, and then..."
